title: Who Is Responsible After a Suspected Dog Attack?
summary: A Hong Kong case shows why responsibility can be hard to prove.

1.content:
A 27-year-old woman died after a suspected dog attack in Yuen Long, Hong Kong, in September. Police said she was cycling home when dogs followed her. They said animals were believed to have caused her injuries.

Afterward, officials caught eight unattended dogs nearby. Three had microchips, but their licences had expired. One registered keeper was prosecuted over a licence and failing to control a dog in public.

This does not prove which dog caused the woman's injuries. Authorities had not conclusively identified which dogs were responsible. When a dog has no clear owner nearby, who must keep people safe? A microchip shows registration, but the facts still need investigation.

vocabulary.definition: without a person watching or controlling it
small electronic devices placed under an animal's skin for identification
having a duty to deal with something or its results

quiz.question: What had authorities not conclusively identified?
options: Authorities had not conclusively identified which dogs were responsible.
They had not learned that dogs can have microchips.
They had not found any dogs in the area.

2.content:
A fatal suspected dog attack in Yuen Long raised questions about stray dogs and responsibility. A 27-year-old cyclist was found with serious injuries after dogs followed her on September 19. Police said animal bites or claws were believed to have caused the injuries, but the cause of death needed further examination.

During a five-day operation, officials caught eight unattended dogs nearby. Three were microchipped, but their licences had expired. One registered keeper was prosecuted for allegedly failing to keep a valid licence and control a dog in public. The prosecution did not identify which dog caused the death.

A microchip links a dog to a registered keeper, but it may not show who was caring for the dog at the time of an incident. A dog may be abandoned, allowed to roam, or passed to another person without updated records.

Responsibility depends on evidence about the dog, the people connected to it, and local law. Regular feeding can create a difficult question, but it does not automatically prove legal responsibility. Public safety and animal welfare both matter.

vocabulary.definition: causing death
formally accused in court of breaking a law
an event, often one that is unusual or serious
facts or information used to show what happened

quiz.question: What did officials find about three of the unattended dogs?
options: None of the three had ever been registered.
All three were proved to have caused the death.
Three were microchipped, but their licences had expired.

quiz.question: Why does a microchip not settle every responsibility question?
options: A microchip proves that a dog is dangerous.
A microchip means a dog can never be abandoned.
A microchip links a dog to a registered keeper, but it may not show who was caring for the dog at the time of an incident.

3.content:
Two fatal dog cases in Hong Kong in August and September renewed debate about safety, ownership, and stray animals. In the Yuen Long case, police said a 27-year-old cyclist was chased by dogs and later died. They believed animals caused her injuries, but the cause of death still needed further examination in the first report.

The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department and police later caught eight unattended dogs. Three had microchips but expired licences. One registered keeper was prosecuted for alleged licensing and dog-control offences. Those facts do not identify which dog caused the injuries or establish responsibility for her death.

Official figures measure the number of stray dogs caught. They were 463 in 2023, 425 in 2024, and 398 in 2025. These capture figures do not measure how dangerous all free-roaming dogs are. They cannot by themselves explain two recent tragedies.

A dog described as stray may still have a human history. It may have been registered, abandoned, regularly fed, or informally cared for. A microchip is evidence of registration, not automatic proof of control at the time of an attack. Any decision about liability must depend on the evidence and the law that applies. Cities must protect people while also treating animals humanely.

vocabulary.definition: made people start discussing something again
the system of giving official permission or registration
moving around without being kept in one place or controlled
legal responsibility for harm or loss
in a kind way that avoids unnecessary suffering

quiz.question: What do the 2023 to 2025 figures measure?
options: The number of dog owners found guilty in court each year.
Official figures measure the number of stray dogs caught.
The number of fatal dog attacks each year.

quiz.question: What do the capture figures not show by themselves?
options: They do not show that microchips exist.
They do not show that Hong Kong has any dogs.
These capture figures do not measure how dangerous all free-roaming dogs are.

quiz.question: What is a microchip in this case?
options: A microchip is evidence of registration, not automatic proof of control at the time of an attack.
It is a device that decides legal liability.
It is automatic proof of control at the time of an attack.

title: What Happens When a City Hides Its Trains Underground?
summary: Tainan plans green public space while keeping its historic station.

1.content:
A railway runs through Tainan, a city in Taiwan. The tracks make it hard to cross the city. People on foot or bikes cannot always go straight across. Now the city is moving its trains underground, below the streets.

The new line is expected to open on October 17. Later, workers will remove the old tracks. The city plans to use that space for trees and paths. People could walk or ride bikes there. The old station building will stay beside the new underground station.

But the work is not all finished. Opening the new line does not mean the green paths are ready. Changing the space above will take more time.

vocabulary.definition: the two metal lines that trains move along
below the ground
small routes for people to walk or ride along

quiz.question: Are the green paths ready when the new line opens?
options: No, the green paths still need more work.
Yes, all the green paths are ready.
No, the city has no plans for green paths.

2.content:
In Tainan, Taiwan, a railway connects the city from north to south but makes travel between its eastern and western neighbourhoods difficult. Trains and the structures around the tracks create barriers for people walking or cycling. Moving the railway underground could help reconnect these areas.

An 8.23-kilometre underground section is expected to open on October 17. The project received approval in 2009. Eventually, it will remove 23 railway crossings and related structures. However, workers must still remove old tracks and restore roads after underground services begin.

The city plans to turn the former railway route into a green corridor about 30 metres wide, with walking and cycling paths and landscaped areas. It could link neighbourhoods, schools and public facilities. This remains a plan, rather than a finished park.

Meanwhile, the historic station building, rebuilt in 1936, will remain beside the new underground station. Possible future uses include reading spaces and exhibitions. The change offers a chance to improve daily journeys while keeping a connection to local history.

vocabulary.definition: things that block movement or make it difficult
to return something to a useful or good condition
a long narrow area that connects different places
public displays of objects or information for people to see

quiz.question: Why could moving the railway underground help the city?
options: It would stop all trains from travelling through Tainan.
It could make travel between separated neighbourhoods easier.
It would move every resident closer to the station.

quiz.question: What is planned for the historic station building?
options: It will be moved to another city.
It will be demolished to make space for the new line.
It will remain beside the new underground station.

3.content:
Tainan's railway illustrates how infrastructure can connect a region while dividing a city. Its north-south route has long supported transport, yet tracks, crossings and associated structures have complicated movement between eastern and western neighbourhoods. An 8.23-kilometre underground section, expected to open on October 17, could begin to change that relationship.

Approved in 2009, the project will eventually eliminate 23 crossings and related structures. However, the first-stage opening is not equivalent to completing the urban transformation. Surface tracks must be dismantled, roads restored and pedestrian facilities improved. The full project is scheduled for completion in March 2031.

Transport authorities plan a green corridor roughly 30 metres wide along the former railway route, incorporating walking and cycling paths and landscaped areas. It could connect neighbourhoods, schools and public facilities, although these benefits depend on subsequent work. The historic station building, rebuilt in 1936, will remain alongside the underground station; reading spaces and exhibitions are among the uses under discussion.

The challenge is therefore both spatial and cultural. Removing a physical barrier creates an opportunity for useful public space, but does not automatically deliver it. Retaining the old station also offers a way to connect daily travel with local history. The project's broader success will depend on what happens above ground after trains move below it.

vocabulary.definition: the basic physical systems, such as railways and roads, that allow a place to function
equal in meaning, effect or value
taken apart in an organised way
happening after something else
relating to how places or objects are arranged in space

quiz.question: What distinction does the article make about the first-stage opening?
options: It begins a change whose surface improvements still require work.
It means the historic station has already become an exhibition space.
It confirms that all surface improvements are complete.

quiz.question: How can the railway connect and divide at the same time?
options: It connects the city culturally but has never supported transport.
It supports north-south transport but obstructs movement between eastern and western areas.
It links every neighbourhood equally but separates all trains from stations.

quiz.question: What will help determine the broader success of the project?
options: Whether the first trains run underground without any future surface changes.
Whether the city removes all reminders of the railway.
Whether the released land becomes useful public space while history remains connected to daily life.

title: AI Uncovers Old Flaws, Sending Websites Offline Worldwide
summary: Researchers report two serious weaknesses in PHP, software used to build many websites.

1.content:
AI tools helped researchers find two old problems in PHP. PHP is software that helps many websites work. These problems stayed hidden for years, according to the report.

The problems could let attackers control some website computers and steal private information. This does not mean every website was attacked. Some organisations took websites offline to reduce the risk. Fixes are now available.

Website owners should ask their hosting company or developer about the PHP fixes. Updating WordPress alone does not fix PHP. Most visitors do not need to act now. They should follow advice from services they use. They should also watch for fake messages about the problems.

vocabulary.definition: Not seen or known about.
Not meant for everyone to see.
Made to look real, but not real.

quiz.question: What needs its own security fix?
options: Only WordPress.
Every visitor’s phone.
PHP.

2.content:
Researchers used AI to uncover two serious security flaws in PHP, according to the report. PHP runs on web servers and helps create pages for visitors. Many websites, including those built with WordPress, depend on it.

The researchers said the flaws had remained hidden for years. Under certain conditions, attackers could use them to control affected servers and steal sensitive data. This risk does not mean every website has been hacked. Some organisations temporarily took services offline as a precaution.

Emergency fixes, called patches, were released. Security agencies urged operators to apply them quickly and consider taking websites offline if protection could not be added promptly. Updating WordPress or its plugins alone does not repair PHP itself. Owners whose websites are managed by others should ask their hosting company or developer whether the PHP fixes have been applied.

Most visitors need no immediate action. However, they should follow security advice from affected services and watch for phishing messages. These try to trick people into sharing information. AI can help defenders find weaknesses, but it can also help attackers exploit them.

vocabulary.definition: Computers that provide websites or other services to users.
An action taken to reduce a possible risk.
Software updates that fix problems.
Using deceptive messages to trick people into revealing information.

quiz.question: Why did some organisations take websites offline?
options: To replace every visitor’s computer.
To reduce a possible security risk.
To show that all their data had been stolen.

quiz.question: What should an owner with a managed website ask?
options: Whether visitors have updated their phones.
Whether the website has changed its colours.
Whether the PHP security fixes have been applied.

3.content:
AI-assisted research has exposed two longstanding vulnerabilities in PHP, prompting an international security response, according to the report. PHP runs on web servers and supports many websites, including WordPress-based platforms. The flaws concern the underlying language rather than merely an individual website plugin.

Researchers at Wiz and Calif reported that, under suitable conditions, attackers could exploit the weaknesses to take control of affected servers and steal sensitive data. Some organisations temporarily suspended services as a precaution. Such shutdowns do not establish that those services were successfully compromised, and the reported risk should not be confused with confirmed data theft.

Emergency patches were released, while security agencies urged operators to update promptly or consider temporary shutdowns when protection could not be applied quickly. Updating WordPress or its plugins alone cannot resolve flaws in PHP itself. Owners using managed services should ask their hosting provider or developer whether the PHP fixes have been installed.

The discovery illustrates AI's dual role in security: it can expose bugs that have escaped detection for years, but also accelerate attackers' development of offensive tools. Most ordinary users need no immediate action, although they should follow advice from affected services and remain alert to phishing messages exploiting publicity around the incident.

vocabulary.definition: Weaknesses that could allow a system to be attacked.
Forming the basic layer on which something else depends.
Accessed or controlled without permission.
Having two parts or roles.
Intended to attack rather than defend.

quiz.question: What can be concluded from a precautionary shutdown?
options: An organisation is reducing a possible risk.
Every server has certainly been compromised.
Data theft has definitely been confirmed.

quiz.question: Why is updating WordPress alone insufficient?
options: PHP operates only on visitors’ personal devices.
The flaws affect PHP beneath the website software.
WordPress updates always remove all server protections.

quiz.question: What dual role does the reading attribute to AI?
options: It helps find flaws and can accelerate attacks.
It replaces both website owners and visitors.
It causes every bug and automatically repairs it.

title: Are Skills Becoming More Important Than Degrees?
summary: Singapore's new framework encourages employers to assess abilities, without removing degree requirements.

1.content:
A degree shows that someone has finished university. But it cannot show every skill a person has. On October 19, a new plan in Singapore asked employers to look more closely at what people can do. Employers are the people or companies that give people jobs.

Nelson studied business, not engineering. His employer paid for training and let him learn through real projects. Now he leads a team of engineers. Learning helped him do different work.

The plan gives advice. It does not make companies change their rules. Degrees are still useful, and some jobs need special training. The idea is to consider skills too, including the ability to learn new things.

vocabulary.definition: A qualification someone earns by finishing university study.
An ability to do something well.
Learning how to do a job or activity.

quiz.question: What does the plan ask employers to consider?
options: Only the university someone attended.
Only the number of jobs someone had.
What people can do.

2.content:
On October 19, Singapore's Institute for Adult Learning introduced a plan encouraging employers to focus more on skills. Its Skills-First Framework for Action contains 12 ideas organizations can test, including checking workers' skills regularly and writing job descriptions around the abilities needed.

The framework covers hiring, promotion and training. It offers guidance rather than forcing employers to change. It does not remove degree requirements. A degree remains useful, but it may not reveal everything an applicant can do.

Nelson's experience illustrates the approach. He joined an engineering company after studying business management. When new mapping technology arrived, his employer funded training and gave him real projects. He is now an assistant project manager leading engineers. His progress shows why opportunities to learn matter alongside existing qualifications.

Skills can be demonstrated through projects, work samples or practical tests. These methods may help career changers, but employers must assess people fairly. Degrees still provide knowledge and foundations, and professions such as medicine require formal training and official qualifications.

vocabulary.definition: A structured set of ideas for deciding what to do.
A move to a job with greater responsibility or status.
Someone who asks to be considered for a job or opportunity.
Judge someone’s ability or performance using relevant information.

quiz.question: What does Nelson’s experience show?
options: Professional training was unnecessary for his progress.
Studying business automatically qualifies someone for every engineering job.
Employer-supported learning can help someone take on different responsibilities.

quiz.question: How does the framework affect company rules?
options: It requires companies to remove every degree requirement.
It offers ideas without forcing companies to change their rules.
It requires companies to stop training existing workers.

3.content:
Singapore's Institute for Adult Learning introduced its Skills-First Framework for Action on October 19, encouraging organizations to consider demonstrated ability in recruitment, promotion and training. Its 12 proposed actions include regular skills reviews and rewriting job descriptions around required capabilities. The framework is advisory: it neither abolishes degree requirements nor compels employers to adopt new rules.

Nelson's career illustrates the potential of this approach. Entering an engineering company with a business-management background, he received employer-funded training in new mapping technology and opportunities to apply it on real projects. He now leads engineers as an assistant project manager. The example concerns supported learning and progression, rather than expecting applicants to arrive fully equipped for every responsibility.

As technology reshapes work, qualifications earned years earlier may not capture recently acquired capabilities. Portfolios, practical assessments and experience outside formal education can provide additional evidence. Such methods may widen access for career changers and people without degrees, but assessing performance fairly remains difficult; a short test cannot reveal everything about future workplace effectiveness.

Nor does the approach make university education irrelevant. Degrees can provide substantial intellectual foundations, while some professions require formal qualifications. Employers must also align their actual selection practices with advertised openness. The issue is how credentials, demonstrated skills and the capacity to learn should inform decisions together.

vocabulary.definition: Intended to offer guidance rather than impose a requirement.
Development toward greater skill, responsibility or opportunity.
Collections of work that demonstrate someone’s abilities.
Qualifications or records used as evidence of someone’s suitability.
The ability or potential to do something.

quiz.question: Why is the framework described as advisory?
options: It requires every employer to use an identical hiring test.
It legally prohibits employers from asking for qualifications.
It offers guidance without compelling employers to adopt new rules.

quiz.question: What limitation of practical assessments does the article identify?
options: A short test cannot capture all future workplace effectiveness.
They guarantee that every candidate will be treated fairly.
They can only measure knowledge gained at university.

quiz.question: What is needed beyond advertising openness to skills?
options: Employers must choose applicants only from familiar universities.
Employers must make their actual selection practices consistent with that openness.
Employers must stop considering every formal qualification.

title: Why Are Young Chinese Couples Changing Wedding Traditions?
summary: Their simpler celebration still included about 70,000 yuan in food.

1.content:
A young couple in China wanted a different wedding. They did not use wedding cars, a paid host or a video team. The groom did not go to collect the bride. Instead, the couple focused on good food and their guests.

Their wedding was simpler, but not everything was cheap. They still spent about 70,000 yuan on food. They also traveled to take wedding photos. They chose what mattered most to them.

Some young couples want less stress on their wedding day. Others want to save money. But families may still value old customs. Some couples keep these customs and add their own ideas. A simpler wedding can still feel special.

vocabulary.definition: Two people who are together in a relationship.
People invited to an event.
Ways of doing things that a group has followed for a long time.

quiz.question: What did the couple focus on?
options: A large video team.
Good food and their guests.
Wedding cars and a host.

2.content:
A young couple in China's Zhejiang province chose a wedding without four common extras: collecting the bride, wedding cars, a professional host and a video team. Their September celebration focused instead on food and guests. Chinese media called it a “four no's wedding.”

Large weddings can involve months of planning, many guests and an exhausting schedule. Couples may feel pressure to meet relatives' expectations. Some younger people now prefer smaller gatherings or skip services they do not value. Saving money, reducing stress and expressing their personalities can all influence these choices.

However, simpler does not always mean cheaper. The Zhejiang couple still spent about 70,000 yuan on banquet food in the bride's hometown. They also traveled to Yunnan for wedding photographs. Their choices show a different set of priorities, rather than avoiding every expense.

Customs vary across families and regions. Some parents see ceremonies as signs of respect and connection. Many couples still enjoy traditional weddings, while others combine older customs with new ideas.2

vocabulary.definition: Making someone feel very tired.
Beliefs about what someone should do or what should happen.
Things someone considers more important than other things.
Formal events that mark important occasions.

quiz.question: Why is the Zhejiang wedding not simply a story about spending less?
options: The couple still spent heavily on things they valued.
The couple avoided paying for any food.
The couple kept every wedding service.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the changes in weddings?
options: Some couples are choosing which customs and services to keep.
All young couples have stopped following older customs.
Every family now celebrates in exactly the same way.

vocabulary.definition: The friendly and generous treatment of guests.
Careful use of money to avoid unnecessary spending.
An established practice generally accepted by a group.
The freedom to make decisions for oneself.
Treat something as more important than other things.

quiz.question: What does the couple’s spending illustrate?
options: The couple rejected food and photographs as unnecessary.
A simpler wedding must cost less in every category.
Removing services can coexist with substantial spending elsewhere.

quiz.question: Why distinguish inherited customs from commercial conventions?
options: Every wedding practice has the same ancient origin.
Some familiar services developed with the modern wedding industry.
Modern wedding services are required in every Chinese region.

quiz.question: What broader change does the article identify?
options: Every family has agreed to abandon wedding ceremonies.
Some couples want more say over what makes their wedding meaningful.
All couples now place the same limit on wedding spending.

title: Virtual Pop Stars Have Real People Behind Them
summary: PLAVE used local English to connect with fans at its first Singapore concert.

1.content:
Five singers appeared on screens at a concert in Singapore. Their group is called PLAVE. They come from South Korea. This was their first concert in Singapore, on October 17. The five figures look like cartoon people. Computers make the pictures, but real people sing and move behind them.

Each person wears special equipment. It follows the person's movements. The cartoon figure then makes those movements on screen. The voices come from people too. This is not a show made only by AI, or artificial intelligence.

The group also used local English words. Fans cheered when they heard these words. The pictures were virtual, but the people behind them were real.

vocabulary.definition: Flat surfaces that show pictures or videos.
Things people use to do a job.
Made with computers rather than physically there.

quiz.question: Who sings for the cartoon figures?
options: Robots sing.
Real people sing.
The fans sing.

2.content:
A concert can have virtual singers and still depend on real people. South Korean group PLAVE showed this at its first Singapore concert on October 17, at APEX @ EXPO. Its five members appeared as animated characters on screens.

Behind each character is a human performer. Special equipment tracks the person's movements and transfers them to the screen. This process is called motion capture. The voices also come from people. Seeing a virtual character therefore does not mean watching a performance created entirely by artificial intelligence, or AI.

The digital format allows unusual stage effects. Characters can change clothes instantly or appear on another screen. Yet technology was only part of this concert's appeal.

The performers used Singlish, the local form of English, including expressions such as “shiok” and “steady lah”. Fans responded with cheers. Familiar language helped the group connect with the audience. The show offered a useful distinction: a computer can create an artist's visible form while a person supplies the performance.2

vocabulary.definition: Made to look as if it moves, using a series of images.
Follows and records how something moves or changes.
Immediately, without waiting.
A difference between two things that should not be confused.

quiz.question: What does motion capture do in this performance?
options: It transfers human movements to characters.
It turns audience cheers into music.
It replaces human voices with computer voices.

quiz.question: How did Singlish help the group?
options: It made the characters change clothes.
It removed the need for human performers.
It helped the group connect with local fans.

vocabulary.definition: A situation in which two things appear incompatible.
Independently, without a person directly controlling the activity.
The capacity to adapt or change in different situations.
Involving many carefully arranged details or parts.
Operated by a system with little or no direct human control.

quiz.question: What does the description “virtual” establish here?
options: The artists have a digital visible form.
Every production process excludes AI.
The singing is produced autonomously by AI.

quiz.question: How does the article interpret the response to Singlish?
options: It proves every audience prefers virtual performers.
It suggests shared references can support connection.
It demonstrates that stage effects are unnecessary.

quiz.question: What limit does the article place on its conclusion?
options: It cannot identify any human contribution.
It cannot distinguish animation from automation.
One concert cannot establish all audience preferences.

title: A Woman Plans to Run About 20,000 Kilometres
summary: Ria Xi aims to reach Portugal from Russia in summer 2027.

1.content:
Ria Xi is a woman from Beijing, China. She is running from Asia to Europe. Her plan is to run about 20,000 kilometres. She started in Russia in May 2026. She wants to finish in Portugal in summer 2027.

Her journey will take her through 17 countries. Her route follows old roads once used for trade. People moved goods along these roads between Asia and Europe. The trip is much longer than one race.

An October report says she has run about 7,000 kilometres. She still has a long way to go. She also keeps information about her body and energy. The journey is not finished yet.

vocabulary.definition: A trip from one place to another.
The way you go from one place to another.
To reach the end of something.

quiz.question: Is her journey finished?
options: Yes, she finished in Russia.
No, she is still travelling.
Yes, she is in Portugal.

2.content:
A woman from Beijing is taking a very long journey on foot. Ria Xi plans to run about 20,000 kilometres from Asia to Europe. She started in Vladivostok, a city in eastern Russia, on May 1, 2026. Her goal is to reach Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, in summer 2027.

The planned route crosses 17 countries and follows the ancient Silk Road. This name describes historic trade routes that connected Asia and Europe. According to an October 18 report, Xi had already covered about 7,000 kilometres. That is a large distance, but it is only part of her plan.

Xi previously worked as a technology executive. She has used AI, or artificial intelligence, to help create training plans. During the run, she records information about her body, memory, motivation and energy.

The challenge involves both physical and mental effort. Following her progress means keeping one important difference clear: she is attempting this journey, and has not completed it. Her arrival date remains a goal.

vocabulary.definition: From a time very long ago.
A person with an important job managing a business.
The reason or wish that makes someone act.
Trying to do something difficult.

quiz.question: What does the report say about her progress?
options: She has finished the whole route.
She has not started the run.
She has covered part of the planned distance.

quiz.question: How does Xi use technology for this journey?
options: She uses AI to replace running with a virtual journey.
She uses AI to confirm that she has reached Portugal.
She uses AI to help plan training and records personal information.

3.content:
Ria Xi, a Beijing-born former technology executive, is attempting a run of about 20,000 kilometres across Asia and Europe. She departed from Vladivostok in eastern Russia on May 1, 2026, with the intention of reaching Lisbon, Portugal, in summer 2027. An October 18 report placed her progress at approximately 7,000 kilometres, leaving much of the proposed journey ahead.

Her itinerary spans 17 countries along the ancient Silk Road, a network of historic trade routes linking Asia and Europe. The scale makes this an endurance challenge extending well beyond a conventional race. Yet the distance already covered and the distance envisaged describe different things: one is reported progress, while the other remains an ambition.

Technology forms another strand of the story. Xi has used artificial intelligence to develop training plans and devised a daily test to monitor bodily measurements alongside memory, motivation and energy. These records add a personal account of how prolonged running affects her physical and mental condition. They do not, by themselves, establish conclusions that apply to other runners.

The essential editorial distinction is therefore between an undertaking and an accomplishment. Xi is still on the road, and summer 2027 is her intended arrival window. Reporting the attempt accurately requires preserving that uncertainty, rather than presenting an ambitious itinerary as a completed crossing.

vocabulary.definition: A planned route or schedule for a journey.
The capacity to sustain effort over a prolonged period.
Imagined or expected as a future possibility.
A substantial task or project that someone commits to attempting.
Something that has been successfully achieved.

quiz.question: Why must the two distance figures be distinguished?
options: They represent two separate completed races.
One describes reported progress; the other describes an intended total.
One measures running, while the other measures travel by train.

quiz.question: What limitation applies to Xi’s personal records?
options: They cannot alone support conclusions about other runners.
They establish that training plans guarantee arrival.
They prove that all runners respond in the same way.

quiz.question: How should the summer 2027 arrival be presented?
options: As an intended window whose outcome remains uncertain.
As the date when Xi began running in Russia.
As a confirmed date on which the crossing was completed.

title: Japan Has More Foreign Residents Than Ever
summary: New figures show about 4.28 million, as an aging population leaves businesses short of workers.

1.content:
More people from other countries now live in Japan. On October 16, officials shared new numbers. About 4.28 million foreign residents lived there at the end of June 2026. Residents are people who live in a place. The number is the highest so far. It does not include tourists on short visits.

Japan has more old people and fewer young people. Many businesses need more workers. People from other countries can help do these jobs. But living in Japan for a long time may become harder. AFP reports that Japan made some rules stricter in October. Businesses want better support for foreign residents.

vocabulary.definition: People who live in a place.
People who do jobs.
Help that someone needs.

quiz.question: Why do many businesses need foreign workers?
options: They have too many workers.
They have too many tourists.
They have too few workers.

2.content:
Japan has a record number of foreign residents, according to figures released on October 16. About 4.28 million lived in the country at the end of June 2026. That was about 156,000 more than at the end of 2025. Short-term visitors are not included.

Foreign residents account for roughly 3.5 percent of Japan's population. However, this is a count of residents, not just workers. Japan's overall population is getting older and smaller, making it difficult for businesses to find enough staff.

An immigration expert told AFP that Japan would continue to need workers from abroad. Businesses have asked the government for a wider policy to support foreign residents. At the same time, opposition to immigration has grown.

AFP also reports that Japan tightened some permanent residency rules in October. Permanent residency allows people to live in a country without a fixed end date. The expert warned that tougher rules could make staying less attractive. Meeting demand for workers and supporting residents are connected challenges.

vocabulary.definition: People who live in a particular place.
The people who work for an organization.
Disagreement with or resistance to an idea or policy.
Continuing without a planned end date.

quiz.question: What does the 4.28 million figure measure?
options: Everyone who visited Japan during June.
Foreign residents, excluding short-term visitors.
Only people working in Japanese businesses.

quiz.question: Why might tougher residency rules concern businesses?
options: They could discourage people from staying.
They guarantee more people will settle in Japan.
They remove every limit on short visits.

3.content:
Japan's foreign resident population reached a record 4.28 million at the end of June 2026, according to figures announced on October 16. The total rose by approximately 156,000 from the end of 2025 and represented roughly 3.5 percent of the national population. It excludes short-term visitors and should not be interpreted as a foreign-worker count.

The increase comes as Japan's population ages and contracts. Immigration expert Toshihiro Menju told AFP that labor shortages extend from specialized professions to service jobs. In his assessment, automation and greater participation by women and older workers cannot fully compensate for the shortfall. That is an expert judgment about workforce needs, rather than a conclusion established by the resident total alone.

Businesses have called for a comprehensive approach to supporting foreign residents. Yet political resistance to immigration has intensified. AFP reports that Japan tightened permanent residency requirements in October, including income and Japanese-language expectations. Menju warned that more restrictive rules could weaken the incentive to remain, while low wages and a weak yen could also discourage longer stays.

The tension concerns both recruitment and retention: attracting workers does not automatically persuade them to build lasting lives in Japan. The figures establish a demographic milestone; they do not, by themselves, show how successfully residents are being supported.

title: Why Did Protests in France Turn Violent?
summary: Most people marched peacefully, but clashes and fires shifted attention away from their demands.

1.content:
On October 17, many people marched in France. Students wanted better schools. Workers wanted better pay and help with high prices. Most people were peaceful. They wanted the government to listen.

But some groups fought with police. They started fires and broke into shops. Police used gas and water to control the crowds. In one city, a fire badly damaged the city hall. By October 19, police had arrested more than 2,400 people across France.

Officials blamed groups that wanted to fight. Other people questioned how police acted. There was no single agreed reason for the violence. The fires drew attention away from the problems behind the marches.

2.content:
Hundreds of thousands of people protested across France on October 17. The Interior Ministry estimated 550,000 participants, while organizers put the figure near 800,000. Most marched peacefully, but smaller groups clashed with police, started fires and looted shops.

Students were demanding better school conditions, including more teachers and less crowded classrooms. Workers and trade unions raised concerns about wages, pensions, public services and living costs. These different complaints brought people together for a national protest.

The government blamed radical groups for much of the violence. Critics also questioned police tactics, including tear gas and water cannons. Injuries during earlier student protests had already caused anger. These competing accounts do not establish one explanation for every clash.

A fire badly damaged the city hall in Limoges. By October 19, more than 2,400 people had been arrested nationwide. The prime minister asked some local authorities to introduce limited curfews where further violence was considered likely. The unrest shifted attention from protesters' demands to restoring order.

3.content:
France's October 17 demonstrations united students, trade unions and other protesters around grievances over schools, incomes and public services. The Interior Ministry estimated nationwide participation at 550,000; organizers suggested roughly 800,000. Although most participants marched peacefully, smaller groups engaged in clashes, arson and looting.

Students had protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating buildings. Workers challenged living costs, wages and pensions. Some Yellow Vest participants also joined the demonstrations. That movement began over fuel taxes in 2018 before broadening into concerns about inequality. France's tradition of mobilization helps explain the protests' scale, but does not establish why particular confrontations became violent.

Officials attributed much of the destruction to radical groups arriving prepared for confrontation. Critics questioned police methods, including tear gas and water cannons; injuries during earlier student demonstrations had already intensified anger. These competing accounts should not be mistaken for a single, settled explanation of every incident.

A fire severely damaged Limoges's nineteenth-century city hall, and arrests nationwide exceeded 2,400 by October 19. The prime minister requested limited local curfews where further violence was judged likely. President Emmanuel Macron condemned the destruction and appealed for calm. The unrest redirected debate toward security, potentially obscuring the grievances that peaceful demonstrators had wanted the government to address.

title: Can Dry Ice Clear Southeast Asia’s Toxic Haze?
summary: Indonesia is testing a way to move smoke trapped near the ground.

1.content:
Smoke from fires in Indonesia has made the air dirty. It has reached other countries. Some schools have closed.

Indonesia is trying something new. Planes will drop dry ice over a smoky area. Dry ice is very cold, frozen gas. Officials hope it will help the smoke rise and move away. They do not yet know if it will work.

The dry ice will not stop the fires. Many fires are still burning. Some burn under the ground and are hard to reach. Indonesia is also trying to make rain to help stop them. For now, clean air is still a big problem.

It has already stopped the fires.

2.content:
For months, smoke from fires in Indonesia has spread across Southeast Asia. Schools have closed, and people have stayed indoors. On October 15, Indonesian authorities began a trial in South Sumatra. They planned to release about 1.5 tons of dry ice from planes. Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide.

The experiment aims to move smoke, not put out fires. Usually, warm air rises and carries pollution upward. Sometimes warmer air sits above cooler air near the ground. This is called a temperature inversion. It acts like a lid and traps smoke below. Officials hope dry ice can cool the upper layer and let the trapped air rise. They hope visibility will improve, but the method is unproven.

The fires remain the main source of pollution. Many burn on peatland, where dried plant material can keep burning below the ground. Indonesia is also using cloud seeding to encourage rain and fight the fires. Dry ice may move smoke; cloud seeding aims to make the land wetter.

Harmful material in the air, water, or land.
Keeps something in one place so it cannot easily leave.
Wet land containing partly decayed plants that can burn when dry.

quiz.question: What is the dry-ice trial mainly trying to do?
options: Make peatland dry enough to farm.
Put out every forest fire directly.
Move smoke that is trapped near the ground.

options: Because all warm air rises without stopping.
Because a warmer air layer can trap cooler air and smoke below.
Because planes keep the smoke below them.

3.content:
Indonesia is testing whether dry ice released from aircraft can reduce the haze caused by forest and land fires. On October 15, authorities began a trial over South Sumatra, with planes prepared to release about 1.5 tons of frozen carbon dioxide. They hope to improve visibility from around one to at least five kilometres. This is a target, not a result.

The idea concerns a temperature inversion. Normally, warm air rises and carries smoke upward. During an inversion, a warmer layer sits above cooler surface air, limiting that upward movement. Officials hope dry ice will cool or disturb the upper layer enough for trapped smoke to rise. Whether this works at useful scale remains unknown. This is the country's first trial of the technique for haze.

Even a temporary improvement would not extinguish the fires. Many burn on peatland: layers of partly decayed plants that can dry out after drainage and then burn beneath the surface. Cloud seeding aims to make rain and wet the land. Dry ice targets smoke already in the air; cloud seeding targets the conditions sustaining fires.

The haze has crossed borders, disrupting schools and travel. The trial may offer short-term relief, but preventing fires and protecting wet peatlands address the continuing source of the smoke.

To put out a fire completely.
The removal of water from land.
Keeping something going over time.

The distance between the fires and Singapore.

title: In China, People Are Paying to Feel Less Lonely
summary: Services bring meals, hospital help and conversation to older and younger customers.

1.content:
In China, some people pay someone to visit them. Yang is 91 and lives near Beijing. After her husband died, her home felt very quiet. Now a small team brings her hot meals twice a day. The visitors also stay and talk with her.

Young people use these services too. Some pay a helper to go to hospital with them. Their family or friends may live far away. Others pay someone to walk with them in the mountains.

These visits can help people feel less lonely. But a paid helper cannot take the place of every close friend or family member.

2.content:
In China, people are paying for company as well as practical help. Yang, a 91-year-old woman near Beijing, became lonely after her husband died. Wang Yingwei and his team now visit twice daily with hot meals. They also help with household problems and make time to talk.

Such support is useful when relatives live far away. Many young adults move to other cities for work or study, leaving older parents behind. Yet loneliness also affects younger people who have moved away from home.

In Beijing, 23-year-old Liu Yanyan works as a medical escort: someone paid to help customers during hospital visits. Some customers are in their twenties. Hiring help can feel easier than asking a friend to miss work. Elsewhere, people hire hiking partners for photographs and encouragement.

Paid companionship offers clear expectations about the help provided. However, it raises questions about what friendship means. A reliable visit can improve someone's day, even though professional support cannot replace every close relationship.

In China, paid companionship is turning everyday acts of care into a growing business. For Yang, a 91-year-old widow near Beijing, the service includes hot meals, help with household problems and conversation. Wang Yingwei's team visits twice daily, offering support that may help older customers remain at home longer.

The demand extends beyond older people. As young adults relocate for employment or education, families become geographically separated, while newcomers can struggle to form local connections. In Beijing, medical escort Liu Yanyan accompanies customers through hospital visits; some are in their twenties. Hiring assistance can spare them the discomfort of asking a friend to miss work or feeling obliged to return a favour. Hiking companions offer another version, combining practical guidance with photographs and encouragement.

Researchers suggest that a paid arrangement can feel less complicated than friendship because responsibilities and expectations are clearer. That predictability may be reassuring, although a defined service is different from an intimate relationship.

The broader question is whether commercial companionship supplements personal care or allows families and communities to withdraw from it. The services cannot replace every close relationship, and their wider social effects remain open to debate. title: Did Tesla Really Make a Flying Car?
summary: A new Roadster flew briefly in a test without a person inside.

1.content:
Tesla showed its new Roadster in Texas on October 15. The car left the ground. Jets of gas pushed it into the air. It moved above other cars, turned and came down again. No one was inside the car.

So, is it a flying car? It can fly for a short time. But it cannot fly between cities like a plane. The test showed a jump, not a long trip. Its use on public roads is unproven.

The Roadster is also made to be very fast on the ground. Tesla says it plans to start making the new car in 2028. For now, the flying version is a test, with many questions still to answer.

2.content:
On October 15, Tesla's redesigned Roadster briefly left the ground at a Texas test site. Gas jets lifted and turned the car before it landed. It crossed over other vehicles. There was no person inside during the flying demonstration.

The system uses gas stored at high pressure. When it escapes through nozzles, the gas pushes the car in the opposite direction. This is called thrust. Spacecraft use similar technology. But the Roadster has no wings or large helicopter blades. Its brief jumps are not the same as flying between cities.

Tesla also says the Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than one second. That is a company claim, not a result for every future car. Tesla first announced the new Roadster in 2017 and now aims to begin production in 2028.

There is another limit: leaving the ground may bring aviation rules into play. It is unclear where an owner could legally use the flying system. For now, the Roadster is a sports car that has flown briefly in a controlled test.

Tesla's new Roadster did leave the ground during an October 15 demonstration at SpaceX's Texas test site. A version equipped with cold-gas thrusters rose, turned in the air and landed. It also cleared a row of vehicles. No person rode inside during these maneuvers. The car flew briefly but has not demonstrated ordinary air travel.

The system stores gas under high pressure and releases it through nozzles. The escaping gas produces thrust in the opposite direction, allowing the car to lift and change orientation. A separate suction system helped it drive upside down on a ramp. Neither system makes it equivalent to an aircraft that can carry passengers over long distances.

Tesla says some versions can reach 60 miles per hour from rest in under one second. Independent tests have not established how production cars will perform. The second-generation Roadster was announced in 2017, with deliveries initially expected in 2020. Tesla now targets production in 2028.

Practical use presents another challenge. Aviation experts told WIRED that a car leaving the ground would likely face approval and airspace rules. Elon Musk acknowledged that the flying feature might not be legal everywhere. The test therefore proves a short airborne maneuver under controlled conditions, while passenger use, regulatory approval and delivery remain open questions.

title: Rats Make a Special Sound When They Eat Chocolate
summary: The high sound may be linked to tasty food.

1.content:
Rats make sounds that humans cannot hear. These are ultrasonic calls. Scientists in Japan listened to rats while they ate chocolate, a food the rats liked very much.

They found a special 40-kilohertz call. Its shape looked like an upside-down U on a sound picture. Nearly all of these calls happened within one second of the rats biting or chewing chocolate.

The call was much less common when the rats ate normal food. This may mean that the sound is linked to eating something tasty. But it does not prove that a rat is saying "yum." The scientists recorded pairs of rats, so they could not always tell which rat made each call.

2.content:
Rats use ultrasonic calls, sounds too high for humans to hear. Researchers in Japan recorded pairs of male rats while they ate chocolate. With a computer method, they identified a 40-kilohertz call whose line rose and fell like an upside-down U.

The call was closely timed to eating. In one experiment, 97.2% of the inverted-U calls came within one second of a bite or chewing. The rats made far more of these calls while eating chocolate than while eating regular food. The amount of food they ate was similar in the comparison.

The team also gave rats naloxone, a drug that blocks opioid receptors. The calls became less frequent. Opioid systems help regulate reward-related processes, so this result suggests that the calls may be linked to positive feelings during tasty eating.

However, the study did not prove what a call means. Because two rats lived in each cage, the recordings could not show which individual rat was calling at a particular moment. The sounds may be useful clues, not a direct translation of rat thoughts.

recognized or found after careful study
happening often
parts of cells that receive chemical signals

3.content:
Scientists want ways to study positive emotional states in animals that cannot describe their feelings. Researchers from the University of Fukui and other Japanese institutions studied ultrasonic vocalizations in male rats eating chocolate. A machine-learning method distinguished a 40-kilohertz, inverted-U-shaped call from other calls.

The new call was tightly linked in time to chocolate feeding: 97.2% occurred within one second of biting or chewing. It was also significantly more frequent during chocolate consumption than during regular chow eating, even though the rats ate similar amounts of the two foods. This makes a simple explanation less likely: that the sound is caused only by chewing.

The team gave the rats naloxone, which blocks opioid receptors. It reduced the calls during chocolate eating, and it also reduced chocolate consumption. This finding suggests that the body's opioid system helps regulate the calls, but it does not prove that each call measures pleasure alone.

An important limitation remains. Rats were housed and recorded in pairs, and the researchers could not identify the individual animal making each sound. Calls could relate to feeding, taste, social conditions, or other internal states. The study offers a possible non-invasive behavioral signal for future research, not a way to read a rat's mind.

Van Gogh painted the flowering chestnut trees in May 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, a French town. He died only weeks later, aged 37. Works from this final period attract interest because they are closely connected to the end of his career. Many major Van Gogh paintings are already in museums and are rarely offered for sale.

The painting could sell for about $180 million. This is an estimate, not a sale price. If the bidding reaches that level, it could set a new auction record for Van Gogh. 3.content:
Vincent van Gogh's Chestnut Trees in Blossom has reappeared before a November 18 auction in New York. Hana Bank said financial information was not leaked. That is important, but personal data still matters. A criminal can use a name and phone number to send a scam message that looks real.

People can also combine data from different leaks. One leak may have a phone number. Another may have an address or email. Together, these details can help someone pretend to be you. A data leak does not always mean money was taken, but it can create new risks.

title: South Korean Ship Sails to Europe Through the Arctic

1.content:
A ship from South Korea went to Europe by sea. It did not take the usual way south. It went north through the Arctic, a very cold area near the top of Earth. The ship carried large boxes of goods.

It left Busan, a city in South Korea, on August 22. It stopped at three ports in Europe. Then it came home. It reached Busan again on October 11. The whole trip there and back took 50 days. Fifty days was not the time for one way.

The complete journey took 50 days; that figure is for the trip out and back, not for the crossing to Europe alone.

Near Taoyuan, a city in Taiwan, people changed lights around Lala Mountain. Workers put covers on some streetlights. They also turned some lights toward the ground. The city says it changed more than 400 public streetlights. Roads still need light so people can travel safely at night.

summary: Lava added 32.8 hectares of land in Indonesia.

1.content:
Anak Krakatau is a volcano in Indonesia. In early September, it erupted for about 25 hours. Hot lava flowed toward the sea. The lava cooled and became hard rock.

Indonesia's Geology Agency used satellite pictures to compare the island on August 8 and September 15. It said the volcano grew by 32.8 hectares, or about 81 acres. This means the island had more land after the eruption.

Anak Krakatau, a volcano in Indonesia's Sunda Strait, changed the shape of its island after a long eruption in early September. The eruption ran from late September 4 to early September 6 and lasted about 25 hours. Lava flowed from the volcano toward the sea.

When lava meets seawater, it cools and hardens into rock. The lava cooled and became hard rock. As more rock built up at the edge of the island, the coastline moved outward. Indonesia's Geology Agency said this process added 32.8 hectares, or about 81 acres, to the volcanic island.

The agency compared Sentinel satellite images from August 8 and September 15. The images helped scientists compare the island on August 8 and September 15. On September 23, images also showed two new land formations: one northwest and one southeast of the coast.

The formations were found 760 meters and 495 meters from Anak Krakatau's coast. Scientists confirmed that they exist, but they still need more data. The formations could be new eruption vents, where lava comes out, or piles of material left by the eruption.

Lava flowed from the crater toward the sea, where it cooled into solid rock. Indonesia's Geology Agency said the volcanic edifice, the body of the volcano, expanded by 32.8 hectares, about 81 acres.

The conclusion came from Sentinel satellite imagery. By comparing images from August 8 and September 15, the agency measured a larger land area around the volcano. This is a visible example of land being built by volcanism: molten rock reaches the coast, cools, and adds to the shoreline.

Images from September 23 also showed two new land formations. One was about 760 meters northwest of Anak Krakatau's coastline; the other was about 495 meters southeast. Their line points through the main crater. Officials said the formations exist, but further analysis is needed to tell whether they are new eruption vents or deposits of erupted material.

The name Anak Krakatau means Child of Krakatau. The 1883 Krakatau eruption destroyed Danan and Perbuatan and part of Rakata, creating a caldera. Underwater activity began in 1927, and Anak Krakatau later became a permanent island above sea level. Its growth is real, but volcanic landscapes can also change again through erosion, collapse, and future eruptions.

title: Why Does a Drug’s Shape Matter?
summary: The Nobel-winning work helps make useful medicines.

1.content:
Some molecules have two forms that look like mirror images. They are like a left hand and a right hand: similar, but they do not fit on top of each other. These forms can act differently in the body.

On October 7, the chemistry Nobel Prize went to Henri B. Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan. Their work showed how a chemical reaction can help chemists make more of one mirror form than the other. This helps scientists make medicines with the form they want.

The work gives chemists useful tools. It does not fully explain why life first began to use one form more than the other.

vocabulary.definition: Very small groups of atoms joined together.

Explain exactly how the first living things began.
Make every molecule have two different formulas.

2.content:
A molecule can have two mirror-image forms. They contain the same atoms, but their shapes point in opposite ways, like left and right hands. A molecule’s shape can change how it interacts with other things. One version may smell like mint, while its mirror image may smell like caraway.

This difference matters in medicine. A drug molecule’s two forms can have different effects in the body. The two forms can have different effects in the body. So scientists need ways to make the form that can do the intended job.

Henri B. Kagan, from France, and Kenso Soai, from Japan, shared the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on October 7. Kagan’s research showed that a reaction could favor one mirror form. Later, Soai developed a reaction. It could efficiently produce one form. The work gave chemists powerful tools for making selected molecules and designing medicines.

Living things favor one mirror form of certain molecules. The Nobel-winning research helps explain how chemistry can favor one form, but it does not answer every question about how life first developed this preference.2

title: NASA Will Search for Caves on the Moon
summary: They could help future astronauts find shelter.

1.content:
NASA has chosen new projects for a future Moon Base. One project will look below the Moon's surface for natural tunnels called lava tubes. These tunnels may be places where astronauts could find shelter.

The Moon has very hot and very cold places. It also has harmful radiation and tiny space rocks that can hit the ground. A tunnel under the surface could give better protection. NASA will send an instrument to a place called Marius Hills Pit. It will scan below the ground to see if the pit leads to a large lava tube. NASA has not yet confirmed that there is a useful tunnel there. The project will help teams learn what is safe before people live there.

a place that gives protection

It will scan below the ground to see if the pit leads to a large lava tube.

2.content:
NASA has selected three new investigations to prepare for a sustained human presence at the Moon. One project, called GIMLI, will study the Marius Hills Pit. Its goal is to scan beneath the lunar surface and learn whether the pit connects to a large underground lava tube.

Lava tubes can form when the outside of flowing lava cools while lava continues moving inside. When the lava leaves, it can leave an empty tunnel. On the Moon, an underground space could protect future astronauts from extreme temperatures, harmful radiation, and micrometeoroids, which are very small space rocks.

But a lava tube is only a possibility until it is confirmed. NASA says GIMLI will hunt for subterranean lava tubes; it is not a plan to move astronauts into a cave soon. The information could change later habitat planning if a large, stable void is found.

The other new investigations will monitor hazards and study lunar ice and surface conditions. Together, they are meant to help NASA understand resources, risks, and safe operations before a long-term Moon Base is built.

options: That astronauts need protection from radiation.
That the Moon has a surface.
whether the pit connects to a large underground lava tube.

3.content:
NASA selected three payload suites through its PRISM programme to help prepare for Moon Base, a future sustained lunar outpost. The investigations will study resources, environmental hazards, and natural shelters before NASA sends people to live and work there for longer periods.

The Geophysical Investigation for Mapping Lunar Interior, or GIMLI, will work at Marius Hills Pit. It will scan under the lunar surface to determine whether the pit opens into a large lava tube. Lava tubes are underground spaces created by past volcanic activity. NASA says a confirmed void could offer future astronauts ready-made protection from extreme temperatures, ionizing radiation, and micrometeoroid impacts.

That is a potential benefit, not a confirmed home. The project must first determine whether a large tube exists, and later planners would still need to assess its size, stability, access, and safety. Mapping a possible shelter is different from proving that people can live there.

The other payloads add context. LEMS-SP will monitor the lunar environment, including micrometeoroids and seismic events. DISCO will study ice in micro-cold traps and how the surface behaves during operations. NASA says these results will help reduce risks and support safe, long-term activity at the Moon Base.

title: At 41, Should Ronaldo Still Play for Portugal?
summary: His camp exit and public apology have divided fans.

1.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo is 41. He has played for Portugal for more than 20 years. In September, he left the national team camp after a disagreement with coach Jorge Jesus. Ronaldo later apologized to his teammates and fans. He said the coach had broken a promise. The coach said there was no agreement.

Ronaldo says he still wants to play for Portugal if he is fit. But some fans think the team needs to give younger players more time. The decision is not only about Ronaldo's age. A coach must choose the team, and every player must respect that choice.

At 41, Cristiano Ronaldo is still Portugal's all-time leading scorer. But his place in the national team is under debate after he left a training camp in late September. He had not played against Norway. On October 6, he apologized to teammates and fans for leaving.

Ronaldo said coach Jorge Jesus had promised him playing time, then changed the plan. He also said Jesus failed to explain their private discussion as agreed. Jesus denied making an agreement. These are competing accounts, not an established finding about what was promised.

Ronaldo says he would be available again if he is fit and has served any punishment. Jesus has also left open the possibility of a return. Portugal must weigh his experience against younger players' need for chances. The final decision belongs to the coach and football authorities, and no return has been confirmed.

Cristiano Ronaldo's future with Portugal became a public question after he left the team's camp in Copenhagen in late September. The 41-year-old captain had stayed on the bench against Norway. title: Could Plague Spread Around the World?
summary: Experts cite fast treatment, but WHO says this case remains unclear.

1.content:
Plague is an illness caused by a bacterium. One form, pneumonic plague, affects the lungs and can pass between people in tiny droplets from coughs or sneezes. It can become deadly quickly, so early treatment matters.

A woman who worked at a plague research centre in Siberia died after pneumonia. Her cause is unknown. Reports of plague exposure remain unconfirmed. The WHO says it lacks enough information for a full risk assessment. Experts say a worldwide outbreak is unlikely. People with this form usually become very ill soon after infection, making them easier to find and isolate. Antibiotics can treat plague, and health teams can watch close contacts. Plague still causes local cases.

2.content:
Plague comes from a bacterium. The lung form, called pneumonic plague, can pass from one person to another through droplets from a cough or sneeze. It is dangerous without quick treatment, but antibiotics can work well when given early.

A worker at a research centre in Siberia died after developing pneumonia. Her cause is unknown, and the WHO says it lacks enough information for a full risk assessment. Exposure rumours remain unconfirmed. Experts warn against treating them as proof of plague infection.

Experts say a global outbreak is unlikely because people with pneumonic plague become sick after symptoms begin, often within a day. Their illness is severe and visible, so health teams can find and isolate them and watch their close contacts. People with the disease can receive antibiotics.

A 2017 outbreak in Madagascar caused many cases and deaths, yet it ended without spreading around the world. This shows that even a serious local outbreak can remain limited. It does not mean plague has disappeared: it still occurs in animals and sometimes in people.

3.content:
Pneumonic plague is the form of plague that affects the lungs and can pass between people through droplets. It can be fatal without prompt treatment. Yet experts say a global outbreak is unlikely because transmission begins only after symptoms start. The illness often appears within about a day and is usually severe, giving health workers a chance to spot cases, isolate patients and monitor close contacts. WHO says it lacks enough information to fully assess this specific case.

Treatment also matters. A 2025 trial in Madagascar studied two antibiotics for bubonic plague, the form usually spread by flea bites. The medicines treated 91% and 92% of patients. A small number of cases became pneumonic; with fast treatment, 85% survived. This supports early care but does not promise recovery.

Specialist laboratories also use several safety steps. Researchers wear protective equipment, handle samples inside cabinets that pull air away from them, and use sealed containers when moving samples. These layers make accidental exposure rare, although they cannot make risk zero.

Plague still exists in animal populations, and local human outbreaks can occur. Madagascar's 2017 outbreak caused 2,417 cases and 209 deaths, but it ended without becoming a global pandemic. It shows a dangerous outbreak can remain geographically limited and still cause real harm. Low risk does not make the disease harmless.

title: Should You Avoid Eating Burnt Food?
summary: The human cancer risk is still not clear.

1.content:
Dark toast, chips, and biscuits can contain the chemical acrylamide. It can form when some plant foods are cooked at high temperatures. Frying, roasting, and baking can make more of it. Boiling and steaming usually make little or none.

Scientists found that high doses caused cancer in animals. But researchers do not yet know clearly how much risk acrylamide in normal food creates for people. Human studies have given mixed answers.

So one burnt meal is not a reason to panic. The US Food and Drug Administration says people do not need to stop eating baked, roasted, or fried foods. Eating a varied, healthy diet matters. If you cook potatoes or toast, a lighter golden color can help lower acrylamide.

vocabulary.definition: a substance with its own physical and chemical properties
a chemical that can form in some foods during high-temperature cooking
including many different kinds of food

quiz.question: What is still unclear about acrylamide in normal food?
options: Researchers do not yet know clearly how much risk acrylamide in normal food creates for people.
A lighter golden color can help lower acrylamide.
Frying, roasting, and baking can make more acrylamide.

2.content:
Some foods turn brown through a heat reaction. In plant foods, sugars can react with an amino acid called asparagine. This can form acrylamide, especially during frying, roasting, and baking at high temperature. Potato products, toasted grain foods, and coffee can contain it. Cooking with water, such as boiling or steaming, does not usually form much acrylamide.

There is a reason scientists study it. In animal studies, high doses of acrylamide caused cancer. However, those doses were much higher than levels found in food. Studies of people have not given a consistent answer about whether dietary acrylamide causes cancer.

Measuring a person's acrylamide intake is hard. Questionnaires ask people what food they remember eating, but acrylamide levels can differ between foods and cooking methods. Blood markers may help researchers measure longer-term exposure, yet they have not settled the question.

Food agencies treat acrylamide as a potential health concern and encourage reductions. FDA advice is not to stop eating all fried, roasted, or baked food. A practical goal is a balanced diet and not cooking starchy foods much darker than needed.

vocabulary.definition: an amino acid naturally present in many foods
connected with the food a person eats
written sets of questions used to collect information
including different foods in suitable amounts

quiz.question: Why is it difficult to measure a person's acrylamide intake?
options: Animal studies used lower doses than food usually contains.
Boiling always creates more acrylamide than frying.
Acrylamide levels can differ between foods and cooking methods.

quiz.question: What does the FDA advise about fried, roasted, and baked food?
options: FDA advice is to eat only steamed potatoes.
FDA advice is to avoid every food that turns brown.
FDA advice is not to stop eating all fried, roasted, or baked food.

3.content:
Burnt food has become a simple health warning, but the evidence needs careful reading. Acrylamide is a chemical that can form when sugars and asparagine in plant-based food react during high-temperature, low-moisture cooking. The reaction helps create browned color, smell, and flavor. It is more likely with frying, roasting, and baking; boiling and steaming usually form far less.

The concern is based on toxicology. Acrylamide and its metabolite glycidamide damaged DNA and caused cancer in animal studies at high doses. The European Food Safety Authority says this can be a health concern, particularly because people are exposed to acrylamide in many ordinary foods. Children have higher exposure per kilogram of body weight, it says.

This does not prove that burnt toast causes cancer in people. Human epidemiology is limited and inconclusive. Diet questionnaires often cannot estimate individual exposure well, because amounts vary by recipe, temperature, and cooking time. Smoking also supplies acrylamide and can confuse studies.

Risk reduction is therefore a cautious step, not a guarantee or a reason to avoid every browned food. FDA advises a healthy eating pattern rather than stopping fried, baked, or roasted foods. Cooking starchy food to a lighter color and avoiding unnecessary overcooking can reduce formation, while leaving the human cancer question open.

a promise that something will certainly happen

options: Acrylamide is found only in foods cooked with water.

options: Diet questionnaires often cannot estimate individual exposure well, because amounts vary by recipe, temperature, and cooking time.

title: Japan Makes Risky Fish a Tradition
summary: Fugu safety depends on strict training and rules.

1.content:
Fugu is the Japanese name for several kinds of pufferfish. Some can contain tetrodotoxin, a poison. It can make people ill and be deadly. The toxin is in organs such as the liver and ovaries.

Yet fugu has been part of Japanese culture for centuries. The documentary Gun Fish follows people who work with this food. It shows that fugu is not simply a dare. Safe fugu depends on knowledge, careful preparation, and rules.

In Japan, only trained people prepare fugu in approved places. They must know the fish species and which parts can be eaten. Dangerous parts are removed and kept away from food. Cooking does not remove the toxin. People should never prepare a caught fugu at home.

vocabulary.definition: the Japanese name for several kinds of pufferfish
a poison made by a living thing
a particular kind of animal or plant

quiz.question: What makes served fugu safer?
options: Safe fugu depends on cooking every part for a long time.
Safe fugu depends on preparing a caught fish at home.
Safe fugu depends on knowledge, careful preparation, and rules.

2.content:
Fugu, or pufferfish, is a Japanese delicacy, but it can be dangerous when handled wrongly. Its toxin, tetrodotoxin, affects the nervous system. The amount and place of toxin can differ by fish species and body part. The liver and ovaries can contain high levels.

Japan deals with this risk through training and regulation. Rules are set at the prefectural level, and qualified fugu handlers prepare the fish. To be certified, cooks need to identify kinds of fugu, tell edible parts from inedible ones, and clean the fish safely. Shops that handle unprepared fugu must meet rules for their facilities.

These rules matter because heating, salting, or soaking does not make fugu toxin safe. The dangerous parts must be removed before the edible pieces are served. This is why eating fugu at an approved restaurant is different from preparing a fish at home.

The 2026 documentary Gun Fish follows the world of fugu workers and a chef in training. It asks a wider cultural question: how can skill, shared knowledge, and rules turn a difficult food into a tradition?

vocabulary.definition: a food that is special or valued
an official rule that controls an activity
officially recognized as having the needed skill
safe or suitable to eat

quiz.question: Why can ordinary cooking not make unsafe fugu safe?
options: Heating, salting, or soaking identifies fish species.
Heating, salting, or soaking creates a fugu license.
Heating, salting, or soaking does not make fugu toxin safe.

quiz.question: What do cooks need to do to be certified fugu handlers?
options: To be certified, cooks need to serve every part of the fish.
To be certified, cooks need to identify kinds of fugu, tell edible parts from inedible ones, and clean the fish safely.
To be certified, cooks need to remove food-safety rules.

3.content:
Fugu is one of Japan's best-known examples of a food with built-in risk. The word covers a number of pufferfish species, some of which may contain tetrodotoxin. The toxin can block nerve signals, and poisoning can be fatal. Where the toxin appears depends on species and body part, and the liver and ovaries are particularly hazardous.

The key fact about fugu is not that it is a thrill food. Modern fugu service is controlled. Japan's health ministry identifies the fish types and parts that may be eaten, and forbids sale or service of toxic parts such as liver. The ministry warns that normal cooking methods, including heating, do not destroy the toxin.

Responsibility is local as well as national. Nippon.com reports that fugu-handling rules are set at the prefectural level and generally require trained cooks to identify species, separate edible and inedible parts, and clean the fish safely. In Tokyo, businesses handling fugu need an approved fugu handling manager and certified facility.

Gun Fish, a 2026 documentary, follows this world of training and debate. It also raises a broader question about food culture. A hard or potentially dangerous food does not become safe merely because it is traditional. It becomes less risky only through specific knowledge, controlled preparation, and rules that are followed.
