dangerous, especially to health or safety
a duty to make sure something is done properly
a place designed for a particular activity
carefully managed according to rules

title: Some Job Interviews Now Use AI
summary: Candidates want clearer notice of what the technology does.

1.content:
Some job seekers now speak to an AI system in interviews. The system may ask questions by text, phone, video, or a digital person. The experience can feel strange when a digital face looks almost human but not fully natural.

Companies can use AI to ask many people the same questions and organize their answers. But candidates should know what the system is doing. It may help a recruiter, or it may score part of the interview.

Not every AI interview looks at a person's face or voice. HireVue says its current AI scoring uses the transcript of what a candidate says, not facial expressions or tone. AI can make hiring faster, but people also worry about fairness and privacy.

vocabulary.definition: a meeting where an employer asks a person about a job
a written record of spoken words
the right to control personal information

quiz.question: What does HireVue say its current AI scoring uses?
options: It decides every job interview without any human help.
HireVue says its current AI scoring uses the transcript of what a candidate says, not facial expressions or tone.
It uses a candidate's facial expressions and tone.

2.content:
More job seekers now meet AI systems early in hiring. An AI interview can use text messages, a phone call, a video chat, or a digital avatar on screen. The avatar's almost-human face may make people uncomfortable. This reaction is sometimes called the uncanny valley.

Greenhouse surveyed 2,950 active job seekers in the United States, Britain, Germany, Ireland, and Australia. Greenhouse said 63% of U.S. respondents had been interviewed by AI. It also said 38% had left a hiring process because it included an AI interview.

Companies may use AI to ask large numbers of people the same questions and give recruiters a structured record of answers. Still, candidates may not know how their answers are being used. Greenhouse said 70% of U.S. respondents were not clearly told beforehand that AI would evaluate them.

AI interviewing does not mean every system judges faces, eye movements, or tone. HireVue says its AI-scored video assessments analyze the transcript of what a candidate says. It says they do not use facial expressions, body language, appearance, background, or tone of voice.

vocabulary.definition: a digital character that represents a person or system
strange in a way that makes people feel uncomfortable
organized in a clear and planned way
to judge the quality or value of something

quiz.question: What did Greenhouse say about U.S. respondents?
options: Greenhouse said 63% of U.S. respondents had been interviewed by AI.
Every U.S. respondent preferred an AI interview.
No U.S. respondent had left an AI hiring process.

quiz.question: What transparency problem did Greenhouse report?
options: Greenhouse said 70% of U.S. respondents were not clearly told beforehand that AI would evaluate them.
All candidates received a full technical report before the interview.
Every candidate knew exactly how AI would score them.

3.content:
AI is becoming more visible in job interviews at the screening stage. Candidates may interact with a chatbot, an automated phone system, a video tool, or an on-screen avatar. In China, reports during the autumn hiring season said an AI digital interviewer gave some candidates an uncanny-valley reaction: the face seemed human but unnatural.

A 2026 Greenhouse survey of 2,950 active job seekers included 1,200 U.S. respondents. Unless stated otherwise, its release said the findings referred to the U.S. group. It found 63% had been interviewed by AI, 38% had left a hiring process because it included an AI interview, and 70% were not clearly told in advance that AI would evaluate them.

These results do not tell us what every AI interviewer measures. Some systems may only collect or organize answers, while others score parts of an interview. HireVue says its AI-scored video assessments analyze a transcript of the candidate's spoken words. It does not use facial expressions, body language, appearance, background, or tone of voice.

The policy issue is growing. The EU AI Act lists systems used to recruit, filter applications, or evaluate candidates as high-risk. Separate EU guidance says using emotion-recognition AI in recruitment is prohibited. Candidates can ask whether AI will be used, what it assesses, and how human reviewers take part.

people who answer questions in a survey
likely to need special care because mistakes can cause serious harm
the process of finding and hiring workers
technology that tries to identify a person's feelings

It says all hiring AI is completely banned.
The EU AI Act lists systems used to recruit, filter applications, or evaluate candidates as high-risk.

title: Why electric cars might be making some passengers feel sick
summary: Reports are mixed, and the research is still limited.

1.content:
Some people say they feel sick when they ride in an electric car. The BBC spoke to passengers who noticed this. But it does not happen to everyone. Some people say they feel less sick in electric cars.

Experts say a car can make people feel sick when body signals do not match. The eyes, the inner ear, and the body send messages to the brain. In a car, the brain uses these messages to understand movement.

Electric cars can speed up or slow down quickly. Their braking can also feel different. This may be one reason some people feel unwell. However, research on this question is still limited.

vocabulary.definition: people travelling in a vehicle who are not driving
to be the same or work well together
the action of slowing or stopping a vehicle

quiz.question: What does the report say about feeling sick in electric cars?
options: It happens only to drivers.
It does not happen to everyone.
It happens to every electric-car passenger.

2.content:
Some people told BBC News that they felt more motion sick as passengers in an electric car. Other people said electric cars did not make them sick, or even made them feel better. So the reports are mixed.

Motion sickness can happen when sensory cues do not agree. Your eyes may see one kind of movement, while the inner ear and body feel something different. The brain has to compare these messages. If they do not match, a person may feel sick.

Electric cars can accelerate and slow down quickly. Regenerative braking can also change how a car feels when the driver lifts off the accelerator. These features may affect some passengers, but they do not prove that an electric car causes sickness.

Driving style and a person's own risk can matter too. Researchers are studying the question, but the evidence is still limited. More careful studies are needed to understand why some people feel sick and others do not.

vocabulary.definition: movement from one place or position to another
signals that give information
to begin moving faster
facts or information that support an idea

quiz.question: What can happen when sensory cues do not match?
options: A person may feel sick.
A driver learns a new route.
A car becomes quieter.

quiz.question: What does the reading say about the evidence?
options: The evidence proves every electric car causes sickness.
The evidence shows driving style never matters.
The evidence is still limited.

3.content:
BBC News heard from some passengers who said they feel more motion sick in electric vehicles. But the report also found many people who do not have this problem, and some who feel less sick in electric cars. The news is about reports from some passengers, not a rule for everyone.

Motion sickness is linked to a mismatch in sensory cues. The brain uses what people see, what the inner ear senses, and what the body feels to understand movement. If these messages do not agree, the brain may have trouble judging what is happening. This can lead to nausea or dizziness.

Electric vehicles have features that may change a ride. They can have quick acceleration and deceleration. Regenerative braking slows a car when the driver lifts off the accelerator. Some passengers may notice repeated slowing. These changes may be one factor, but they do not explain every case. Driving style, road conditions, and a person's own susceptibility can matter too.

Experts quoted by the BBC said the research is still limited. A small study can explore a possible cause, but it cannot settle the question for all cars and all people. Better evidence will need to compare different vehicles, passengers, and driving conditions.

vocabulary.definition: connected with information from the senses
the feeling that you may vomit
the act of becoming slower
able to recover energy while slowing a vehicle
a greater chance of being affected by something

quiz.question: What three sources does the brain use to understand movement?
options: Only the speed shown on a screen.
Only the sound of the car engine.
The brain uses what people see, what the inner ear senses, and what the body feels to understand movement.

quiz.question: How does the reading say regenerative braking slows a car?
options: Regenerative braking slows a car when the driver lifts off the accelerator.
Regenerative braking removes all movement from the car.
Regenerative braking makes every passenger feel sick.

quiz.question: What is the careful conclusion of the report?
options: Electric cars always cause motion sickness.
Experts quoted by the BBC said the research is still limited.
Only road conditions can affect motion sickness.

title: China Adds Trains for Golden Week
summary: About 13,000 passenger trains are planned each day.

1.content:
China's railway holiday travel period runs from September 23 to October 8. It covers the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays. China Railway plans about 13,000 passenger trains each day. This is a peak timetable for a very busy time.

More trains can help people travel to visit family or take trips. Some high-speed trains will run at night. Other trains can have extra cars. In Shanghai, railway stations expect millions of passenger departures during the holiday rush.

Fast trains are useful, but a busy railway also needs good timing. Trains must arrive, leave, and carry people safely. Stations need enough open waiting rooms and clear ways for passengers to move. The goal is to keep the whole system moving.

vocabulary.definition: a plan that shows when transport services run
people or vehicles leaving a place
connected parts that work together

quiz.question: What is the goal for the busy railway system?
options: The goal is to run only one fast train each day.
The goal is to keep the whole system moving.
The goal is to close waiting rooms at night.

2.content:
The 2026 rail holiday travel period in China lasts 16 days, from September 23 to October 8. China State Railway Group expects high demand because trips for tourism, family visits, and leisure happen at the same time. It plans a peak timetable with about 13,000 passenger trains each day.

This is an example of capacity. Capacity does not only mean how fast one train travels. Capacity includes how many trains the network can run. It also includes how many passengers fit on each train and how quickly a station can manage arrivals and departures. Adding more cars or linking two trainsets can increase space without building a new line.

Railway operators are using night high-speed trains and extra sleeper services on selected busy routes. They use ticket and waitlist data from the 12306 platform to adjust capacity and ticket allocations. In Shanghai, stations plan extra trains and may keep waiting rooms open overnight.

These steps do not make every trip shorter. Instead, they aim to make the system more reliable when many people want to travel at once.

vocabulary.definition: the amount that a system can carry, hold, or handle
a group of connected routes or services
amounts of something that are given to particular uses
able to work well and as expected

quiz.question: Besides speed, what can railway capacity include?
options: Capacity includes the color of every train.
Capacity includes closing all station entrances.
Capacity includes how many trains the network can run.

quiz.question: Why do operators use ticket and waitlist data?
options: They use ticket and waitlist data to cancel all night trains.
They use ticket and waitlist data from the 12306 platform to adjust capacity and ticket allocations.
They use ticket and waitlist data to make every train faster.

3.content:
The scale of China's 2026 Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day rail travel is not only a tourism story. The 16-day travel period runs from September 23 to October 8, and China State Railway Group expects 284 million passenger trips. Its peak plan calls for about 13,000 passenger trains per day. At Shanghai Hongqiao during busy periods, reporting says a train arrives or leaves roughly every five minutes.

Moving so many people depends on system capacity. Train speed matters for a trip, but it is only one part of capacity. A railway must also fit services through shared track, turn trains around, assign platforms, board passengers, and recover from small delays. A busy station can become the limit even when trains are fast.

The operator plans several ways to expand capacity temporarily: night high-speed trains, additional sleeper services, linked trainsets, and extra carriages. Shanghai rail stations expect 8.53 million departures and will add 146 pairs of trains on popular routes. They also plan to monitor ticket availability and waiting-list data so capacity can be changed where demand is strongest.

The lesson is not that railways can remove every queue. It is that a transport network works best when its parts flow together. Frequency, clear passenger routes, well-timed schedules, enough space, and fast recovery can make a large holiday movement more manageable.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of demand that a transport system can handle
the raised areas at a station where passengers get on or off trains
the separate passenger vehicles that make up a train
how often a service happens
possible to control or deal with

quiz.question: What is China Railway's peak plan for passenger trains?
options: Its peak plan calls for about 13,000 passenger trains per day.
Its peak plan calls for one passenger train every five hours nationwide.
Its peak plan calls for no night high-speed trains.

quiz.question: Why can a busy station limit a railway system?
options: A busy station makes every train travel at the same speed.
A busy station removes the need for platforms.
A busy station can become the limit even when trains are fast.

quiz.question: What can make a large holiday movement more manageable?
options: Only making one train travel as fast as possible can make a large holiday movement manageable.
Frequency, clear passenger routes, well-timed schedules, enough space, and fast recovery can make a large holiday movement more manageable.
Closing extra train services can make a large holiday movement manageable.

title: Earth's Core May Change Day Length
summary: The changes are only a few milliseconds.

1.content:
A day is often called 24 hours. But Earth does not turn at exactly the same speed all the time. Over many years, a day can become a few milliseconds longer or shorter. A millisecond is one thousandth of a second, so people do not feel this change.

Scientists have a new idea about why this happens. Deep inside Earth is a solid inner core. Around it is a very thick rocky layer called the mantle. When the inner core changes its movement a little, it may pull on the mantle. This can change the mantle's rotation a little too. Then the length of a day changes. The study says this may be an important reason for these tiny changes.

vocabulary.definition: the movement of something as it turns around
the thick rocky layer inside Earth under the crust
very short times equal to one thousandth of a second

quiz.question: What does the study say may change the length of a day?
options: When the inner core changes its movement a little, it may pull on the mantle.
People can feel Earth's day become longer every morning.
The mantle stops turning around Earth once a year.

2.content:
We use 24 hours as the length of a day, but Earth's rotation is not perfectly steady. On long time scales, the change can be a few milliseconds. The new research looks at broad changes that last many decades.

Earth has several layers. The mantle is a rocky layer about 3,000 kilometres thick that includes the crust. Far below it are a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. The core and mantle can exchange angular momentum, a property of moving, turning objects. When one part changes speed, another part can make a small opposite adjustment.

The researchers studied how the inner core moves compared with the mantle. The inner core is not a perfect sphere. Its shape and the uneven mass in the mantle can create a weak gravitational torque, or turning force. Their model suggests that this torque is the main driver of multidecadal day-length changes from 1964 to 2019. Electromagnetic and topographic forces at the core-mantle boundary may resist the change. The result is a possible explanation, not a direct view of Earth's center.

vocabulary.definition: not changing much
connected with turning around a point or line
connected with the force that pulls masses together
a force that causes something to turn

quiz.question: What kind of day-length changes did the new research examine?
options: Changes caused by every sunrise.
The new research looks at broad changes that last many decades.
Changes measured during one school day.

quiz.question: What does the model suggest about gravitational torque?
options: Their model suggests that this torque is the main driver of multidecadal day-length changes from 1964 to 2019.
It lets scientists directly see Earth's center.
It makes Earth's inner core a perfect sphere.

3.content:
A day is commonly set at 24 hours. Yet Earth's rotation is never perfectly constant. Scientists can detect millisecond changes. Causes differ by time scale. This Nature study covers broad, multidecadal changes.

The authors, Huifeng Zhang and Mathieu Dumberry of the University of Alberta, used reconstructions of inner-core rotation and flows in the liquid core. Their analysis covers 1964 to 2019. It supports an explanation in which the solid inner core exerts a gravitational torque on the mantle. The inner core is slightly uneven rather than perfectly spherical, and it can become misaligned with uneven mass patterns in the mantle. That misalignment creates a small turning force.

Angular momentum is exchanged between the core and mantle. A tiny change in the mantle's rotation can change day length. The researchers found that gravitational torque may be the leading cause of the multidecadal pattern, while electromagnetic and topographic torque at the core-mantle boundary mainly resist it. Their result depends on the accuracy of the inner-core and core-flow models. It is not a final answer to every rotation change.

The model also suggests that the inner core may deform viscously over only a few years. This solid region can slowly change shape under force. The work gives scientists another way to study Earth's deepest interior, which cannot be observed directly.

vocabulary.definition: staying the same over time
scientific estimates of past conditions made from available evidence
not lined up in the same direction
connected with electricity and magnetism
in a slow, flowing way under force

quiz.question: What time period does the authors' analysis cover?
options: Their analysis covers 1964 to 2019.
The first 24 hours after Earth formed.
Only the year 2026.

quiz.question: Why can a small inner-core movement create a gravitational torque?
options: The mantle is outside Earth's atmosphere.
The inner core is slightly uneven rather than perfectly spherical, and it can become misaligned with uneven mass patterns in the mantle.
The inner core is perfectly spherical and has no uneven shape.

quiz.question: What limitation do the researchers give for their result?
options: It directly observes Earth's deepest interior.
It proves every short-term rotation change has one cause.
Their result depends on the accuracy of the inner-core and core-flow models.

title: Scientists Are Giving Coral Reefs Underwater Umbrellas
summary: Simple shades helped some heat-stressed corals keep or regain colour.

1.content:
Scientists in Florida put simple shades over brain corals in the sea. The shades were like underwater umbrellas. They blocked about 60% of sunlight. This helped corals during very hot water.

Corals are animals. Tiny algae live inside them and make food from sunlight. Too much heat and strong light can harm this partnership. Corals may lose algae and turn pale. This is called bleaching.

During the test, shaded corals bleached less. Some got their colour back after scientists added shade. Shade cannot cool the ocean. It may be most useful for rare or important corals during a heat wave.

vocabulary.definition: things that block light from the Sun
very small plant-like living things that can make food from light
when a coral loses colour and turns pale

quiz.question: What can the underwater shades not do?
options: Shade cannot cool the ocean.
The shades cannot block any sunlight.
The shades cannot be placed in the sea.

2.content:
Researchers tested underwater shades at Newfound Harbor in the Florida Keys. They put 20 shades over communities of two kinds of brain coral. The shades were made with PVC pipe, foam, and special cloth.

The shades blocked about 60% of sunlight. From August to November 2024, the researchers watched the colour of the corals. During that time, sea temperatures were above the local bleaching threshold for at least 61 days.

The shaded corals showed less bleaching. Some corals had already started to turn pale before the shades arrived, but they recovered colour after they were shaded. Nearby corals without shade were used for comparison.

The shades are a small-scale solution. They cannot protect every reef or cool the ocean. The team found that the shades stayed clean and needed little care. Researchers say they may help save high-priority corals, such as large or rare corals, during dangerous marine heat waves.

vocabulary.definition: a point where something begins to change
an act of looking at things to see how they differ
became healthy or normal again
something judged to be especially important

quiz.question: How much sunlight did the shades block?
options: The shades blocked all sunlight.
The shades blocked about 60% of sunlight.
The shades blocked no sunlight.

quiz.question: Why are the shades not a solution for every reef?
options: The shades are too bright for every reef.
The shades make the ocean hotter.
The shades are a small-scale solution.

3.content:
A Florida research team tested 20 underwater shades over communities of two Atlantic brain coral species. The experiment took place from August to November 2024 at Newfound Harbor in the Florida Keys. The shades reduced the amount of sunlight reaching coral by 60%.

The test happened during a serious marine heat wave. Sea temperatures were above the Florida Keys bleaching threshold of 30.5°C for at least 61 days. Shaded corals showed less bleaching, and some that had already turned pale recovered colour after the shades were added.

Corals depend on microscopic algae that live in their cells. Heat and strong sunlight can damage this relationship. But the exact reason for colour change is still uncertain. An independent scientist noted that the paler unshaded corals may have changed the amount of chlorophyll in their algae, rather than losing algae faster. The study also could sample only the edges of corals, not the sunniest tops.

The shades do not cool seawater and cannot cover all reefs. The shades may protect high-priority corals during heat waves. This includes large or rare corals. Researchers still need to study long-term effects, such as whether shaded corals stay stronger against disease and can reproduce.

vocabulary.definition: so small that it needs a microscope to be seen clearly
a green material that helps plants and algae use light
not involved in the study or group being discussed
a level of special importance
to make new living things of the same kind

quiz.question: What did the shades reduce in the experiment?
options: The shades reduced all heat in the seawater.
The shades reduced the amount of sunlight reaching coral by 60%.
The shades reduced the number of coral species.

quiz.question: What remains uncertain in this study?
options: The shades were placed under water.
Corals need sunlight to live.
The exact reason for colour change is still uncertain.

quiz.question: What is a realistic use for the shades?
options: They may cover every reef with shade.
They may cool every ocean on Earth.
The shades may protect high-priority corals during heat waves.

title: Slackliner Crosses Line Between Seoul Buildings
summary: Jaan Roose walked 160 metres above central Seoul.

1.content:
On October 1, Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose crossed a 160-metre line between two buildings in central Seoul, South Korea. The line was about 120 metres above the ground. It was Korea's first urban highline performance.

A slackline is a flat, flexible band, not a hard rope. It can move and sway. Roose used his arms and body to stay steady as he walked across it.

Our bodies also work hard to help us balance. The brain gets signals from the eyes, the inner ear, and muscles. These signals help us know where our body is. If signals do not match, people can feel dizzy.

vocabulary.definition: a flat band that people walk on for sport
to move slowly from side to side
messages that give information

quiz.question: What helps people know where their body is?
options: Signals from the eyes, the inner ear, and muscles.
A hard rope under their feet.
The height of the buildings.

2.content:
On October 1, Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose crossed a 160-metre line between the Koreana Hotel and the Dong-A Media Center in central Seoul. The line was about 120 metres above the ground. News reports called it Korea's first urban highline performance.

A slackline is different from a tightrope. It is a flat, flexible band. It can bend and move under the athlete's feet. Even a light wind can make it sway, so the athlete must keep making small body changes.

Balance is not only about your feet. Your eyes show you where you are. The inner ear senses movement and helps the brain know how the head is moving. Muscles and touch sensors also send information to the brain.

The brain puts these messages together. Then it helps the body keep a steady position. If the messages do not work well together, a person may feel dizzy or unsteady. That is why walking on a moving line is such a hard sport.

vocabulary.definition: able to bend or move easily
a person who does sport
a change of place or position
not firm or balanced

quiz.question: Why can a slackline be hard to walk on?
options: It can bend and move under the athlete's feet.
It is always made from hard metal.
It never changes in the wind.

quiz.question: What does the inner ear help the brain know?
options: The inner ear tells the brain how tall the buildings are.
The inner ear tells the brain which sport to play.
The inner ear senses movement and helps the brain know how the head is moving.

3.content:
On October 1, Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose completed a 160-metre highline crossing between two buildings in central Seoul. He walked between the Koreana Hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, about 120 metres above the ground. It was described as Korea's first urban highline performance.

Highlining uses a flat, flexible line that can move under a walker. This makes the sport a clear example of balance in action. A walker watches the line and the space around it, makes quick changes with the arms and legs, and tries to keep a stable posture. Wind can add another challenge by making the line sway.

The body uses several systems to keep balance. The eyes give information about the world around us. The vestibular system in the inner ear senses head movement and gravity. Muscles and touch sensors in the legs report what the body is doing. The brain combines these messages to control posture during movement.

If these signals disagree or do not work well, a person can feel dizzy, unstable, or as if they are moving. Roose's crossing shows why balance is more than strong feet. Balance needs the eyes, inner ear, muscles, and brain to work together again and again.

vocabulary.definition: an event where someone shows a skill
the way a person holds their body
connected with the inner-ear system for balance
the force that pulls things toward the ground
likely to move or fall

quiz.question: What does the vestibular system sense?
options: The vestibular system measures the length of a slackline.
The vestibular system in the inner ear senses head movement and gravity.
The vestibular system chooses the colour of a building.

quiz.question: What can wind do during highlining?
options: Wind can tell the brain which way to walk.
Wind can add another challenge by making the line sway.
Wind can make the line become a hard rope.

quiz.question: What is the main lesson about balance?
options: Balance needs the eyes, inner ear, muscles, and brain to work together again and again.
Balance needs only strong feet.
Balance depends only on the height of a building.

title: Twelve Long-Hidden Paintings Head to Auction
summary: Their pre-sale estimates total about $450 million.

1.content:
Twelve paintings from a private collection will sell at Sotheby's in New York on November 18. The paintings include works by Vincent van Gogh, Claude Monet, and Paul Cézanne. It is the pre-sale estimate for all twelve paintings: about $450 million.

Some of the paintings have not been shown publicly for more than 50 years. One Van Gogh painting, Châtaigniers en fleurs, has an estimate of about $180 million. An estimate is the price an auction house thinks a work may sell for. It is not the final sale price. Famous paintings do not always hang in museums. A family or private collector can keep a painting at home, in storage, or lend it to a museum.

vocabulary.definition: owned by a person or family, not by the public
a careful guess about a future price or amount
a sale where buyers offer prices for something

quiz.question: What does the $450 million figure mean?
options: It is the price of one painting by Claude Monet.
It is the final sale price for all twelve paintings.
It is the pre-sale estimate for all twelve paintings: about $450 million.

2.content:
On November 18, Sotheby's will auction twelve paintings in New York from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection. The group includes work by Van Gogh, Cézanne, Monet, and other artists. Sotheby's says the collection has pre-sale estimates of about $450 million.

The largest estimate is about $180 million for Van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs. Cézanne's Arlequin has an estimate around $120 million. An auction estimate is not a promise; the final price depends on what buyers offer during the sale.

The paintings belonged to a private collection and were mostly bought in London in the 1970s. Some were kept in a private collection and not shown publicly for 50 years or more. A private owner can keep art at home, store it, lend it to a museum, or show it only rarely.

That is why a famous painting can disappear from public view without being lost. The auction will bring these works back before the public, but it does not mean a museum will buy them. The winning buyers will decide where the paintings go next.

vocabulary.definition: a sale in which people compete by offering prices
an expected price, not a guaranteed result
belonging to an individual or family rather than the public
in a way that people can see or know about

quiz.question: What does an auction estimate tell buyers?
options: The auction house has already sold every painting.
An auction estimate is not a promise; the final price depends on what buyers offer during the sale.
A museum must buy the paintings after the sale.

quiz.question: Why had some paintings not been publicly shown for decades?
options: Some were kept in a private collection and not shown publicly for 50 years or more.
No one knew that Van Gogh and Monet were artists.
They were destroyed during the 1970s.

3.content:
An important private collection will be sold at Sotheby's in New York on November 18. It contains twelve Impressionist and modern paintings, including works by Vincent van Gogh, Paul Cézanne, and Claude Monet. Sotheby's places the combined pre-sale estimates at about $450 million.

The leading lot is Van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs, estimated at about $180 million. It was painted in May 1890, after Van Gogh arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise. Cézanne's Arlequin is estimated around $120 million. Sotheby's says the two paintings could set auction records, but that is a prediction, not a result.

The paintings were collected in the 1970s by Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. Some of the works have not been seen on public exhibition for 50 years or longer. Reuters reported that five paintings were shown at Sotheby's in London, while the rest were being shown digitally before selected works travel to galleries worldwide.

A private collection is art owned by an individual or family rather than a museum. Private owners may store a painting, show it at home, lend it to an exhibition, or keep it away from public view. title: Cockpit Attack Forces Flight to Make Emergency Landing
summary: All 174 passengers reached safety after the diversion.

1.content:
A flydubai plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv on September 30. During the flight, there was a serious incident in the cockpit, where the pilots sit. The plane made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

The airline said there was an altercation, or a serious fight, in the cockpit. The crew secured the plane and landed it safely. All 174 passengers and the crew were reported safe. The captain and first officer were hurt and taken to hospital. The plane sent emergency signals during the event. Saudi officials are investigating what happened. The reason for the fight has not been officially established. A second plane later took the passengers to Tel Aviv.

2.content:
Flydubai flight FZ1073 left Dubai for Tel Aviv on September 30 with 174 passengers. It later diverted to Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia after a serious cockpit incident. Flydubai said an altercation occurred in the flight deck and that crew members secured the aircraft.

Flight-tracking data showed a sharp descent during the emergency. The aircraft went from about 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet in about one minute, according to Flightradar24 data reported by the Associated Press. It then reached Tabuk safely.

The plane first transmitted 7700, an international code for a general emergency. It later sent 7500, which signals unlawful interference with an aircraft and can include a possible hijacking. These codes show controllers that an aircraft needs urgent attention; they do not, by themselves, explain the cause.

Saudi Arabia's safety center has opened an investigation. The airport said the captain and first officer were injured and went to hospital. The airline arranged another flight for passengers. Officials have not established a motive, and reports about an attempted crash remain unconfirmed.

Flydubai flight FZ1073, travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, on September 30 after a cockpit emergency. Saudi Arabia's National Transport Safety Center has opened an investigation.

Associated Press reporting, citing Flightradar24 data, said the Boeing 737 Max 8 descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet in about a minute. title: Vermont Homes Form a Virtual Power Plant
summary: Their batteries help during outages and busy hours.

1.content:
Thousands of homes in Vermont have batteries. These batteries can keep lights on when a storm cuts the power. But they can also work together.

The local power company, Green Mountain Power, can use some stored energy when many people need electricity. This group of home batteries is called a virtual power plant. It is not one big building. It is many small batteries linked by software. The company says more than 5,000 customers are now part of the system. Before a possible storm, the company keeps power in the batteries for the homes. At busy times, the shared energy can reduce pressure on the electricity grid. This may lower costs and reduce the need for polluting power plants.

connected by technology instead of being in one real place

options: The company keeps power in the batteries for the homes.
The grid stops carrying electricity to every customer.
The company removes all batteries from homes.

2.content:
A power plant is usually one large place that makes electricity. In Vermont, Green Mountain Power is building a different kind of resource. It links stored energy in thousands of homes, batteries, and devices. Together, they form a virtual power plant, or VPP.

The system does not create electricity by itself. Instead, software coordinates energy that is already stored. During times of peak demand, when electricity use is very high, the company can draw on part of that energy. Customers still keep reserve power, especially when bad weather could cause outages.

As of July 2026, GMP said its VPP could provide 110 megawatts of power. More than half came from home energy-storage systems. The company said its network sent 90 megawatts of stored energy during a July heat event and saved customers about $6 million in one peak hour.

GMP says the growing system has helped it permanently close two fossil-fuel peaker plants. The VPP may make the grid cleaner and cheaper, but it still depends on customers joining, usable batteries, and careful grid management.

the highest point or time of use
a supply kept for a future need
using coal, oil, or natural gas for energy

It sends all home batteries away during storms.

quiz.question: What did GMP say its network did during the July heat event?
options: The company said its network sent 90 megawatts of stored energy during a July heat event and saved customers about $6 million in one peak hour.
The company said it built two new fossil-fuel peaker plants.
The company said it stopped every Vermont power outage forever.

3.content:
Green Mountain Power is expanding a virtual power plant built from distributed energy resources. Its network combines home batteries, utility-scale batteries, electric-vehicle chargers, flexible commercial buildings, and hydropower. Software coordinates them when the grid needs help.

GMP said that, as of July 2026, more than 5,000 customers had more than 10,000 batteries in its programmes. The VPP had 110MW of capacity, with more than half coming from residential storage. This figure measures how much power the system can deliver, not a claim that the VPP produces electricity like a conventional generator.

During a July heat event, GMP said it deployed 90MW of carbon-free stored energy and saved an estimated $6 million in one peak hour. The company says its storage network has allowed it to permanently close two peaker plants, which are usually used only at high-demand times. Those fossil-fuel plants can be expensive and polluting.

For households, the same batteries can offer backup during outages. GMP says it takes steps to preserve home backup when weather is forecast to cause outages. The model still has limits: its benefits depend on enough customers enrolling, equipment working, software coordination, and rules that let utilities use distributed resources. It is a way to manage existing energy more flexibly, not a complete replacement for every part of the power system.

title: Cat Cancer Study May Benefit Pets and People
summary: Nearly 500 tumors reveal shared genetic clues across species.

1.content:
Scientists studied cancer samples from almost 500 pet cats in five countries. They looked for genetic changes that help tumors grow. Many of the same cancer-related genes are also found in people and dogs.

One example is a gene called FBXW7. More than half of the cat breast tumors in the study had a change in this gene. A similar change is linked with human breast cancer.

The team also tested some medicines on cat tumor tissue. Certain drugs worked better on samples with the gene change. But this was a test on tissue, not on living cats. Researchers hope the findings will help veterinarians improve care for cats and may give human cancer research useful clues too.

2.content:
An international team analyzed cancer tissue from almost 500 domestic cats in five countries. The scientists searched for genetic changes that help tumors begin and grow. They found that many cancer-driving genes in cats are also known in human and dog cancers.

One example came from mammary tumors, which grow in breast tissue. The most common driver gene in the cat tumors was FBXW7. More than half of the samples had a mutation in that gene. In people, a similar mutation in breast cancer is linked with a worse outlook.

The team also tested chemotherapy drugs on tumor samples. Some drugs worked better on cat mammary tissue with the FBXW7 mutation. This result came from tissue tests only; it does not show that the drugs will work in living cats or people.

Cats may still offer useful clues because they naturally develop cancer and often share homes and environmental exposures with people. The study could support more personalized treatment for pets and point scientists toward questions about human cancer. Any treatment benefit for either species will need further study.

3.content:
An international study mapped genetic changes in cancers from almost 500 domestic cats across five countries. Researchers found that many genes that drive feline tumors are also involved in cancers in people and dogs. The findings may help veterinary medicine and human cancer research, though they do not establish a ready-made treatment.

The clearest example involved mammary, or breast, tumors. FBXW7 was the most common driver gene in the cat mammary samples, and more than half carried a mutation in it. In people, mutations in FBXW7 are associated with a worse prognosis in breast cancer. Similarities appeared in several other cancer types too.

Scientists tested chemotherapy drugs on cat tumor tissue. Some drugs were more effective in samples with the mutated FBXW7 gene. However, this result came from tissue in a laboratory; it does not show that the drugs will work in living cats or humans. Clinical research would be needed to answer that question.

Cats naturally develop cancer and often share environments with people, so they may help researchers explore how genes and surroundings interact. The study also created a genetic resource for future work. In a two-way approach sometimes called One Medicine, knowledge from veterinary studies could inform human research, while treatments developed for people might eventually be evaluated for pets. title: Milky Way’s First Microblazar Aims a Jet Toward Earth
summary: The distant system may accelerate extremely energetic particles.

1.content:
Astronomers have identified the first known microblazar in the Milky Way. It is a binary system: a black hole and a massive star orbit each other. The black hole pulls gas from the star. Some gas forms a hot disk, while some shoots out in narrow jets.

One jet points almost along our line of sight. This direction makes the system look unusually bright, but it does not mean Earth is in danger.

Radio images also show the jet hitting a cloud of gas and dust. Scientists think this area may speed up tiny particles to nearly the speed of light. They are studying the system to learn how such powerful particles form.

vocabulary.definition: Made of two parts or objects that are linked.
Narrow, fast streams of matter or energy sent out into space.
Very small pieces of matter.

quiz.question: Why does the microblazar look unusually bright?
options: One jet points almost along our line of sight
The star has stopped orbiting the black hole
The system is inside Earth’s atmosphere

2.content:
The first known Milky Way microblazar, IRAS 18293−0941, is a black hole and a massive star orbiting every 11 days. The black hole pulls gas from the star into a hot, spinning disk. Some gas is then fired into space in narrow jets from its poles.

One jet points very close to Earth’s line of sight. Fast-moving radiation aimed toward us can appear brighter, like a flashlight pointed toward your eyes. This effect helps explain why distant blazars look so bright. The alignment is not a danger to Earth.

Radio images show the jet crossing about 100 light-years of space before hitting a dense cloud of gas and dust. At a bright spot there, the jet may accelerate particles to nearly the speed of light and very high energies. The spot also matches a gamma-ray signal.

Researchers describe the system as a potential particle accelerator. More observations will test how the jet heats the cloud and whether it links to the nearby high-energy source.

vocabulary.definition: Turning around a central point.
Energy that travels through space as waves or particles.
Having many things packed closely together.
Possible or able to happen, but not yet certain.

quiz.question: How does the black hole get material for its disk and jets?
options: It takes matter from Earth’s atmosphere
It collects water from the molecular cloud
The black hole pulls gas from the star into a hot, spinning disk

quiz.question: What did the radio images reveal before the jet reaches the cloud?
options: The jet had already left the Milky Way
the jet crossing about 100 light-years of space before hitting a dense cloud of gas and dust
The jet stopped moving near the star

3.content:
A newly identified Milky Way microblazar lets astronomers study blazars normally seen around supermassive black holes in distant galaxies. The object, IRAS 18293−0941, is a binary system: a black hole about ten times the Sun’s mass and a massive star orbiting one another roughly every 11 days. Gas pulled from the star forms a disk; some then escapes as narrow jets from the black hole’s poles.

One jet is aligned very close to our line of sight. Because its material moves at relativistic speeds, radiation directed toward Earth can appear unusually bright. This beaming effect is one reason blazars are so luminous. The alignment is an observing geometry, not evidence that Earth is threatened.

Radio observations trace the jet across roughly 100 light-years before it meets a dense molecular cloud. The impact region is bright, and researchers report that it coincides with a gamma-ray signature. They propose that the jet may accelerate particles there to energies near a petaelectronvolt, or PeV.

The evidence points to a promising accelerator, but the exact link between the jet, the gamma rays and the highest-energy cosmic particles remains a research question. The team plans more observations of the hot spot. Studying this microblazar in detail may help explain how energetic particles are produced elsewhere in the Milky Way and in far more distant galaxies.

Happens or appears at the same place or time as something else.
Something that increases the speed or energy of particles.

options: Its star produces no radiation

options: the exact link between the jet, the gamma rays and the highest-energy cosmic particles remains a research question

Whether the system contains a star

title: Beijing Glass Walls Endanger Migrating Birds
summary: A Wangjing office complex is testing stickers after repeated collisions.

1.content:
In September, a birdwatcher in Beijing found a tiny Arctic warbler dead beside an office building in Wangjing. She was excited to see this bird for the first time, but sad that it had died.

The birds probably hit the buildings’ large glass walls. Glass can reflect trees, clouds, or blue sky. Birds may think the reflection is a real place to fly. Clear glass can also show plants on the other side, so a bird may try to pass through. The bird is not careless; glass walls are new in nature’s long history. Close patterns across the outside of glass can help birds see a barrier. One large sticker may leave too much open space.

vocabulary.definition: a small songbird, often seen during migration
to send an image of something back from a surface

quiz.question: Why might a bird fly toward glass?
options: Birds may think the reflection is a real place to fly.
They are trying to land on one sticker.
They cannot see trees at all.

2.content:
A dead Arctic warbler beside an office complex in Beijing’s Wangjing area was the first sign of a wider problem. The birds were likely hitting reflective or transparent glass.

Glass can mirror trees and sky, or let birds see plants beyond a window. Either way, the surface may look like a safe route. Researchers say the risk is not simply carelessness: birds evolved long before large glass walls existed. A nationwide Chinese citizen-science project surveyed 3,078 buildings from 2021 to 2023. Migratory and smaller birds were more likely to be recorded as victims, and buildings with more glass had more collisions.

Autumn migration can bring many young birds through cities. A Chinese study found nighttime lighting was linked with higher collision risk in autumn, but the overall lighting effect was only marginal. To help, guidelines recommend visible patterns across the outside of glass, with gaps no larger than five centimeters. One hawk-shaped sticker is not enough. A new study found that indris open their mouths wider for higher notes. Researchers looked at 83 videos of 19 wild indris. They compared the animals' mouth movements with the pitch of their songs. The link between wider mouths and higher pitch was strong.

This pattern is consistent with formant tuning. The mouth and throat act a little like a tube. When their shape changes, the sound can resonate differently. A better match between the voice and the vocal tract may make a high note more powerful and help it travel farther.

Trained opera singers use a similar technique. The finding does not mean an indri is an opera singer. It shows that animals and humans can use similar body changes when they face a similar sound problem: how to make a high note carry through a large space.

Formants are resonance frequencies shaped by the vocal tract: the mouth and throat. When an indri opens its mouth wider on a high note, it changes that tube-like space. This can bring a resonance closer to the sound being produced, which can increase vocal power and help a call carry farther. The study describes a link between mouth opening and pitch; it does not mean that every indri song works exactly like a human performance.

The comparison is useful because both species face a physical problem: how to be heard at a distance. Human and lemur lineages split roughly 70 million years ago, Reuters reported. CFCs were used in products such as refrigerators, air conditioners, and spray cans. They can remain in the atmosphere for decades. Sunlight can break them down and release chlorine atoms. The atoms can take part in reactions that destroy ozone again and again.

Solomon found that Antarctica's extreme cold creates polar stratospheric clouds. Their surfaces help activate chlorine. When sunlight returns in spring, ozone destruction speeds up. Scientists' evidence helped lead to the 1987 Montreal Protocol.

The treaty later reached 197 United Nations member states and reduced CFC concentrations. Measurements show the ozone hole is forming more slowly. Still, recovery will take decades, and wildfire smoke or CFC leakage could slow it.

Solomon later showed that very cold polar stratospheric clouds provide surfaces for reactions that activate chlorine. When spring sunlight returns, those reactions accelerate ozone destruction.

Evidence from several research groups helped prompt the Montreal Protocol in 1987. It progressively controlled ozone-depleting substances and gave financial assistance to developing countries adopting alternatives. Solomon said the agreement had been signed by 197 United Nations member states. His goal resembles a finish line that keeps moving away. Reports have described trips through the United States, China, Japan, Europe, the Middle East and Latin America, but an exact global total will always change.

That is why the story works as more than a coffee fact. Winter's project turns an ordinary routine into a way of seeing the world. title: Ancient Clay Beads Hold Children’s Fingerprints
summary: Natufian ornaments reveal makers from 15,000 years ago.

1.content:
Archaeologists studied tiny clay ornaments made up to 15,000 years ago. The objects came from Natufian sites in what is now Israel. They were made before farming and pottery became common in the region.

The small beads and pendants still hold fingerprints from the people who shaped them. Researchers found about 50 prints from adults, children and teenagers.

The ornaments were made from clay and shaped into small discs, rings and other forms. Some looked like plants. A child's fingerprint makes the past feel close: long ago, young people were learning to make things with their hands, too, in daily life.

2.content:
A fingerprint can turn an ancient object into a human story. Researchers studied 142 small clay beads and pendants from Natufian sites in what is now Israel. The ornaments are between about 11,650 and 15,000 years old.

The Natufian people were hunter-gatherers living before agriculture and pottery became widespread in the region. Yet they already used clay to make personal ornaments. The pieces included discs, rings, cylinders and bead shapes that copied plants such as barley, wheat, lentils and peas. Some were colored with red ochre.

Researchers identified about 50 fingerprints. By comparing the width of the fingerprint ridges with a modern experimental dataset, they estimated that adults, children and teenagers worked with the clay. Five ornaments had prints linked to children or younger people.

This does not show exactly what each child was taught or why every ornament was made. But it offers direct evidence that young people were makers, not only watchers. The study suggests that making ornaments may have been a shared activity where skills and social values passed between generations.

3.content:
Small clay ornaments from the Natufian culture have preserved an unusually personal kind of evidence: the makers' fingerprints. A study examined 142 beads and pendants from Israel, dating from about 15,000 to 11,650 years ago. The objects were made before agriculture and pottery became widespread.

The ornaments included discs, rings, cylinders and forms that resemble plants, including barley, wheat, lentils and peas. Some carried a red ochre coating. Their surfaces also retained fingerprints and palm prints from the people who pressed, pinched and shaped wet clay.

Researchers measured the mean ridge breadth of about 50 prints against modern data. Their analysis identified makers from different age groups. Five of the six ornaments carrying fingerprints were attributed to children or subadults; the other was linked to a young adult or adult female. Clay can shrink as it dries, so the study treats these age estimates carefully, not as exact identities.

The finding does not let archaeologists reconstruct one family's day. It does, however, provide direct evidence that children participated in making personal ornaments. That matters because the objects were part of shared symbolic practices in early settled communities. A small fingerprint does not answer every question about the past, but it connects an abstract culture with a person who once pressed a finger into soft clay.

title: Why Do World Leaders Meet at the UN?

1.content:
This week, world leaders are meeting in New York at the United Nations. About 130 presidents and prime ministers will come. They will speak about problems.

The meeting is called the General Debate. Leaders talk about wars, climate change, trade and new technology such as AI. The United Nations has 193 member countries. Each country can have a voice there.

The UN cannot make every country do what it wants. Countries often disagree. But the meeting is useful. Leaders can talk in smaller meetings, too. They may discuss peace, food, trade or help for people in danger. Talking does not always bring an agreement. But it can be harder to solve a problem when countries do not talk at all.

2.content:
Nearly 130 heads of state and government are expected in New York for the United Nations General Assembly's High-level Week. The General Debate runs from September 22 to 28. Leaders explain priorities to a global audience.

The UN has 193 member states, and each one has a vote in the General Assembly. That gives small countries a chance to speak with large powers. Leaders are expected to discuss wars, climate action, trade and artificial intelligence. These problems cross borders, so one country cannot always manage them alone.

Still, the UN is not a world government. The General Assembly can make recommendations, but it usually cannot force countries to follow them. The Security Council has stronger power over peace and security. Its five permanent members can use a veto to block a decision.

The speeches are only part of the week. Leaders and diplomats also hold bilateral meetings, meaning meetings between two countries. They may disagree in public but still need to discuss aid, security or trade. A meeting cannot promise peace. It can keep communication open when agreement is difficult.

The agenda is broad because the problems are connected. Wars, climate change, trade disruption, pandemics and artificial intelligence can affect people beyond one border. The General Assembly gives all 193 member states one vote, so a small island state can speak on the same stage as a major power. Its resolutions usually express collective views or recommendations rather than laws that countries must obey.

This structure explains a common frustration. The UN cannot act like a world government and order countries to end a war. The Security Council can make stronger decisions, but a negative vote from any of its five permanent members can block a decision. When powerful countries have conflicting interests, a shared response can be hard.

Yet the speeches are only one purpose of the gathering. Ministers and diplomats schedule bilateral conversations between two governments. They can raise humanitarian aid, trade, prisoners or ways to prevent a crisis from growing. These talks may not create an immediate agreement, but they create contact. In a divided world, that diplomatic space remains valuable: many problems cannot be managed by one country alone.

title: Habits in Your 30s Can Support Healthy Ageing

Your thirties can be a good time to build healthy habits. A BBC Future report says that exercise, regular sleep, healthy food and less alcohol may support better health later in life. These habits cannot stop ageing or promise that a person will never become ill.

Strong muscles and good movement can help people stay active as they get older. A brisk 15-minute walk after a meal is one simple way to move more. Fruit and vegetables can also be part of a healthy diet.

A BBC Future report says the habits people build in their thirties may affect how well they age. Researchers focus on this decade because muscle strength, bone density and metabolism can begin to change gradually. Health does not suddenly decline at 30, but it can be a useful time to establish routines.

Exercise is important. Experts say that aerobic fitness, flexibility and muscle strength can help people remain mobile and independent later in life. Activities such as walking, cycling, tennis and badminton can add movement. Even a brisk 15-minute walk after a meal can be a practical first step.

Sleep and food matter too. Going to bed and waking at similar times can support a regular sleep pattern. Eating more fruit and vegetables while reducing ultra-processed foods is also widely linked with better health. Reducing excessive alcohol use and not smoking are other helpful choices.

The evidence does not offer guarantees. People have different bodies, jobs and family responsibilities. But healthier habits in midlife are associated with lower risks of cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline and frailty decades later.

Maintaining movement can support mobility and independence as balance matters more. The report mentions cycling, tennis and badminton, but it also stresses that small actions count: a brisk 15-minute walk after a meal may be an accessible way to start.

Sleep, nutrition and other daily behaviours matter alongside exercise. Consistent sleep timing may support the body's circadian rhythm. Diets rich in fruit and vegetables and lower in ultra-processed foods are associated with better health. The report also points to reducing excessive alcohol use, avoiding smoking and maintaining good dental care. These are linked to lower long-term risks, not guaranteed outcomes.

Studies such as the Framingham Heart Study and the Nurses' Health Study have associated healthier midlife lifestyles with lower risks of cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline and frailty. title: Can You Wash Underwear and Socks Together?
summary: For healthy households, detergent and a full wash are usually enough.

1.content:
Can underwear and socks go in one washing machine load? For most healthy households, they usually can. A normal wash with detergent removes dirt, oils and many microorganisms. Clothes do not need to be completely sterile to be safe to wear again.

Water, movement, detergent and rinsing work together during a wash. Drying matters too, because many microorganisms grow better in damp places. Underwear and socks should both be washed after each wear.

There are exceptions. Use extra care if someone has vomiting, diarrhea, a contagious skin infection or a weakened immune system. Very muddy clothes and delicate fabrics may also need to be washed separately.

2.content:
Many people worry that washing underwear and socks together will move germs from one item to another. For most healthy households, a normal wash load is usually safe. The American Cleaning Institute says they can wash laundry with detergent at ordinary temperatures, including cold water.

A washing machine does not make clothes sterile. It removes dirt, body oils, smells and enough microorganisms for normal use. Water and movement loosen material. Detergent holds oils and dirt in wash water, and rinsing carries much away. Drying fully matters because damp conditions support microbial growth.

Sorting by color, fabric and dirt level can matter more than separating underwear from socks. Dark socks may affect white underwear, and delicate items may need a gentler cycle. Clothes covered in mud may be better washed separately from lightly soiled clothes.

Extra precautions make sense when someone has vomiting, diarrhea, a contagious infection or a weakened immune system. Follow fabric labels, use the warmest suitable setting, and dry items completely. People with athlete's foot should keep feet dry, change socks daily and avoid sharing socks or towels.

Laundry is cleaning, not sterilisation. Water loosens and dilutes soil; movement helps remove it; detergent suspends oils; rinsing carries material away. Heat adds microbial reduction only when fabric can tolerate it. Full drying matters because microorganisms grow more easily in damp conditions.

The CDC says it is safe to wash a sick person's dirty laundry with other items when handled and cleaned properly. Still, vomiting, diarrhea, a contagious skin infection or a weakened immune system may require more caution. Follow care labels, choose the warmest appropriate setting, and dry items completely.

Sorting still matters. Very muddy socks can make it harder to clean lightly soiled clothes. Dark dyes, rough fabrics and zippers can damage delicate underwear. title: The World Now Has More Older Adults Than Young Children
summary: Falling birth rates and longer lives are reshaping the global population.

1.content:
For most of history, the world had more very young children than older adults. That has now changed. A new report from the U.S. Census Bureau says people aged 65 and over became more numerous than children aged 0 to 5 between 2020 and 2025.

In 2025, about 852 million people were 65 or older. They made up 10.5 percent of humanity. By 2060, that share could reach 19.6 percent, or almost one in five people. Two main forces explain the shift: people live longer, and families are having fewer children. The news does not mean older people are a problem. The change has two main causes. People are living longer because of improvements in health care, education and living conditions. At the same time, fertility—the average number of children a woman has—is falling in many countries. In 2023, more than 71 percent of the world's population lived where fertility was at or below the replacement level of about 2.1 children per woman. Asia shows the trend clearly. Japan was the oldest country in 2025, with 29.7 percent of its people aged 65 and over.
